Question: Some Quora users claim that all finite state games, like tic-tac-toe, chess or Go, if played optimally by both players, would end in draw. Is that so? In particular, what's known about chess and Go?
Answer: I play Go using New Zealand rules, where the komi is 7.0. That means it’s entirely possible to get a draw - you simply need a score of 177 to 184 on the board. Now that might only happen 2% of the time with human-level opponents but you’re talking about optimal play. Given the top AIs think 7.0 is about right, I’d frankly be surprised by anything other than a draw under perfect play. New Zealand is unique in having a whole number of points for komi, with 6.5 and 7.5 both popular in other countries. It is technically possible to share an single common liberty in a seki and so create a draw, but I’ve only seen it once and that was on 9x9. Another possibility is that one player, seeing the situation is hopeless, could create a triple ko and invalidate the game. That wouldn’t work in NZ which uses the superko rule, but we’ve already eliminated NZ rules. My guess though is that under perfect play, Go would be a forced win for white assuming over 7 points komi, a draw with 7 points, and a forced win for black if komi is under 7.

Question: Has anybody on Quora read the entirety of the published volumes of Knuth’s ‘The Art of Computer Programming’ (TACP), which (as of 2024) would include volume 4B? Is reading - or at least attempting to read - TACP a worthwhile pedagogical endeavor?
Answer: There’s read, and there’s read. I’ve read TAOCP because it was described as some sort of holy grail. I learned assembly (6502) as a child and had picked up a couple other architectures before starting uni, so MIX was well, just another instruction set. Job done, box ticked. But… well, when I was doing my PhD, I would devour a paper every day just to keep up the breadth of my knowledge. These were typically conference papers of eight pages and it would take me a little under an hour. At the same time I was writing my literature review with a deep dive into a couple areas and for this I would take the same conference papers I was reading daily and truly understand one. Implement it from scratch, reproduce its results, read its references. Think (and experiment) with how it could have been done differently. I’d often contact the authors and bounce ideas off them. The point I’m making is you can read a paper and get something out of it in an hour, or read exactly the same paper for a month. Knuth’s work… it’s dense. It’s easy enough to skim read, but to truly master it… would be a lifetime of work. I also strongly disagree with Knuth on the use of MIX. THere was a study of teaching arithmetic to children after calculators became commonplace. One school of thought was kids should master arithmetic, and then be allowed a calculator. The other is they should be given a calculator from the start, and with encouragement they’d learn what the calculator does. I believe the second school of thought has it right here - you make things easy to get started and enable people to dig deeper. Knuth makes every step a slog, on the logic that if you get through it then you must have mastered the material. Also I came to the books comfortable in assembly. A younger programmer from a different generation… would spend half their time just learning basic coding. They’d be getting nothing in terms of abstract ideas because their brain would be too busy with the mechanics. So no, if you want to deeply master fundamental algorithms, then I wouldn’t go that route. If you want to push yourself out of your comfort zone… and force yourself to do something the hard way, then sure, it’s probably a good choice.

Question: Why, philosophically or mathematically, if the chance of something occurring in any given year is 1%, is the probability of it occurring within 20 years not 20%?
Answer: The chance of it not occuring in one year is 99% The chance of it not occuring in twenty years is 80% The chance of it not occuring in a hundred years is 0% The chance of it not occuring in a thousand years is -900% My favourite thing about proof by contradiction is you don't have to calculate the correct answer, you just have to show the provided answer is wrong and that's far easier. As for why it's wrong…. You'd agree there is some chance of it occuring more than once in twenty years. Some nonzero probability? We know probabilities sum to 100% so that small chance must come from the 20% and/or the 80%. Once you accept those cannot be twenty and eighty, all that's left is the detail of whether 20 is too high or 80. Basically you've fixed your mental model well enough now that I've lost interest. Calculating 20% requires simple arithmetic which kids learn at about eight. Calculating the correct answer requires exponents, which I think get taught at about 13. While essentially everyone in developed countries would have been taught both and more, people start to forget what they don't use and the harder stuff goes first. A proof involving exponents will be beyond many more people than one involving only multiplication.

Question: Can you open a bank account for business when you already have one?
Answer: Yes, but it’s less useful than you might think. With a personal account you can sort-of budget by setting up accounts for different things. That just isn’t realistic with a business, even a small business. You have to use accounting/budgeting software (or have your accountant use it for you). It’s too hard to be compliant with taxes otherwise. Accounting software largely works by taking the money in all your bank accounts and putting it into one big pool. So the only reason to open a second account is when the bank offers different rates/fees that you want to take advantage of. For example you might have an account in each currency you trade, one for general savings, one for savings you know you won’t touch in the next twelve months, and one for day-to-day. Note also that business bank accounts have many features that personal ones don’t, including APIs and multiple authorisations. For example if I’m paying a supplier then I do the whole thing in the accounting software, which talks to the bank via the open banking API. That way all of the controls limiting the amount a staff member can spend or requiring approval for invoices are managed by the accounting software rather than the bank. One upside of multiple accounts, at least where I live, is that transfers between accounts at the same bank are in real time while transfers between different banks occur hourly. We will not release finished jobs for new customers until the money has landed in our bank account and at times that hour delay can be a real problem. PS: Just wanted to give a brief acknowledgement to Wise (formerly TransferWise). Back when I started it was an absolute nightmare dealing in other currencies. It was easy enough to hold cash in order to hedge against exchange rate transfers but they were not real bank accounts in the other country. If you wanted a real bank account then you had to deal with an international bank (we used HSBC) and have at least a nominal legal entity in each country. Transferring money between your bank accounts typically cost $50 plus the exchange rate was lousy for small transfers, so you’d need at least two accounts (a holding account that gets topped up when it is low and a trading account). With Wise it’s about five minutes work to get a bank account in another country, plus they have excellent API support.

Question: What is the significance of the Turing test in the field of artificial intelligence, and how does it contribute to our understanding of machine intelligence?
Answer: We’ve had AI systems since the 1950s and technically even before. They were primitive but every year they got a little better and not just because computers got faster. When I got into the field in the 90s, you’d see a computer doing something such as playing chess and say ‘wow, that computer is intelligent, it has artificial intelligence’. Then you’d learn how the algorithm worked, how it was: a bunch of handcrafted rules to turn a chess position into a score, coupled with making moves at random really quickly. You’d say ‘bah, that’s not intelligence, that’s just very fast search’. Often we’d devise a tricky edge case to highlight how stupid the computer is. People would say ‘ah, that computer is not intelligent because it had to be supplied with handcrafted rules to score a chess position’. Now if it worked out those rules for itself that’d be different, I’d call that intelligent. Then a few years later someone would develop a new algorithm which could do that, and they’d review it and say… ‘well now, yes it can do Chess but see how it basically has the rules built in? Try giving it Othello and it can’t cope. The cycle would repeat every few years as increasingly generalised algorithms came out. Turing was unbelievably brilliant. He saw this all playing out all the way all the way back in the 40s. He said ‘let’s all agree now on something that we all think is intelligent, and when a computer can do that we’ll all be forced to accept that computers are intelligent’. The test itself was poorly written and has a lot of (justified) criticism. Firstly conversational text wasn’t a great choice, secondly it’s poorly phrased in terms of ‘convincing a judge’, and thirdly people effectively cheated by pretending to be non-native speakers of English or similar. But whatever, we’re not here to criticise the test, we’re here to admire that this guy saw in the 1940s that the goalposts were being moved and so nailed them down some seventy years before the test was passed (at least to my satisfaction). how does it contribute to our understanding of machine intelligence? My gut reaction was that it doesn’t, but thinking more… maybe. I remember reading criticism by a guy called Searle and what it boiled down to is ‘computers aren’t intelligent because even if they perfectly imitate intelligence, they are just imitating it’. I really disliked this criticism because it felt too self-fulfilling. “You’re not playing go intelligently, you’re just looking up a series of rules in 500 million parameter dictionary which tells you what to play in certain positions. You’re not conversing intelligently, you’re looking up a series of rules in a 20 billion parameter dictionary which tells you what token to output next”. Meh, whatever. what’s the use in such thinking? Turing’s test bypasses this. If it looks like a duck and it quacks like a duck then it’s a duck. If it looks intelligent and it acts intelligent then it is intelligent - you can’t go defining intelligence in terms of some impossible-to-measure spark.

Question: What are your thoughts on the ethical considerations surrounding the use of artificial intelligence in various aspects of society, and how do you think we can address these concerns moving forward?
Answer: I was really disappointed by the latest EU act. Rather than create a framework that ensures AI should be used ethically, they instead simply banned AI from a bunch of use cases. Further, the ban will eliminate numerous beneficial applications of AI. The whole thing struck me as incredibly naive, like… why are we letting these people make decisions about our future when they don’t understand the technology at all. It’d be like putting a computer programmer in charge of the legal system, I’m sure they’ll try their best but you can guarantee they’ll make a hash of it. AI gives scale, nothing more and nothing less. You can write a blog post yourself without trouble, and using AI you can write maybe a hundred in the same time. Ethics comes up at least three ways: If I was developing a law to keep AI deployments ethical then I’d take a three pronged approach with each prong tackling one of the above points. You need to directly address bad actors; you need to enforce governance safeguards are in place before systems scale; and you need to respect that people cannot cope with change beyond a certain pace. Instead what we got was a bunch of application areas being banned, as if say ‘AI in the workplace’ is inherently dangerous, while ‘AI for relationship-based selling’ is all good. I’m not saying it’s easy, but the approach has to be about governance of implementations rather than banning use cases. There shouldn’t be any banned use cases, there should be requirements to check safety nets: The thing about these are they’re exactly the same protections you’d put in place if you were making a major change that doesn’t use AI.

Far better perhaps, and a few opportunities for saving non-clinical time, but nothing huge. So I don't expect a big change in the demand for doctors, at least in the near future. Give it ten more years and things might be different as nurses’ scope increases. Why bother getting all those years of education when your primary role is empathy? I was involved in a telehealth programme using AI where primary care came from managers at work. The idea was that while service would not be as good, it was a lot better than seeing nobody. Improve the AI and use a nurse rather than a manager, and I think it could be just as good.

Question: Why does New Zealand have 2 time zones?
Answer: Some thirty years ago when I first started using the internet, I was quite confused to discover NZ had two time zones. There was one called NZ which was obvious, and another called NZ-CHAT. I was confused why we had a special timezone just for chatting but I just rolled with it. The internet at the time had a lot of in-jokes and I just assumed I didn’t know this one. I was particularly confused by the timezone being 45 minutes off - I mean who ever heard of a 45 minute timezone difference!? My assumption was the joke was something like “NZers chatted before starting a meeting, so if you arrive 45 minutes later then you’ll skip the chat”. I was really quite naive at the time, but also the Chathams was less well known. At 800 odd kilometers east of Christchurch, it was almost another country. Since then Air New Zealand decided to pull out of a bunch of small regional airports and Air Chathams has stepped in, so I suspect they’re much more recognised now. They even have their own check-in counter at Auckland Airport. There’s actually quite a few islands in NZ. The North and South are obviously the most well known and largest, but then you get Stewart Island, Great (and Little) Barrier Island, Waiheke, D'Urville Island, and obviously the Chathams. Population drops off fast, with roughly 80% of people on the North island, followed by the next 80% on the South island, and so on. There are 730 people living in the Chathams, so they’re doing pretty well to have both their own airline and timezone.

Question: What assumptions did you make to determine how much startup capital you’d need before you launched your business?
Answer: I built a little computer simulation which embedded the assumptions. I looked at cost to acquire, retention rate, spend on first purchase, spend ongoing, and referral rate. I had a bunch of estimates for each number based on other similar businesses, and so I simulated different random settings and looked at the distribution of outcomes. This outcome distribution was effectively the startup capital needed. If I was going to lose $30k in the second year then I'd need an extra $30k of startup capital. I really didn't want to run out of money if the business was going to ultimately succeed so I looked at all simulations that succeeded and made sure I'd saved that much before starting. In hindsight I think it was mostly a waste of time. I'd put too much time into simulating the parts I understood and not enough into the things I didn't. I had staffing issues and I was so busy between working in the business while trying to deal with them that I could see we were missing targets but not what to do about it. Two mistakes I'd fix if I were to ever do it again: firstly borrow less, go cheaper on fitout and stuff. I went with what the simulation said was best, but that meant that when the simulation turned out to be wrong, I was in with very high stakes. Secondly withdraw a personal market salary even when the business is losing money. It's very easy to prop up a business by donating your time, and forcing the payment would have made this much more obvious.

Question: How do I cover the cost when offering benefits to employees in a small business? I have a service based business but I'm not sure how to cover the costs of insurance, vacation days ect if I have to pay out at least 70 percent as an owner.
Answer: The business model for a service provider is dead simple. You get a percentage from each dollar billed, and you have some fixed monthly overheads. To use real numbers, I get 25% of every dollar earned, and my fixed overheads are $30k/month. Some simple arithmetic shows that I hit breakeven at about $1.5m in revenue. If we gross $2m then I make $140k, and if we gross $1m then I lose -$110k. Of course reality is more nuanced. For all your expenses such as insurance, vacation etc you need to work out if they are closer to fixed or to scaling with revenue. My guess is both insurance and vacation scale with revenue - double the staff and you'll double your insurance and vacation costs. So, you'll need to include them in your gross profit percentage. If that means you lose money, well that's too bad. You get to take home the profit at the end of the day, even if that means you work full time for the privilege of losing $110k. One of the more painful realisations I had was that that the setup I most enjoyed, where I managed a team of six, was uneconomic. It was too big for me to work as a consultant as well, while not being big enough to afford me as a manager. The universe doesn't care.

Question: What is the time in which #16840 will earn #2947 of simple interest at 5% per annum?
Answer: Since you've asked the same question twice and nothing else, I'm assuming you have a genuine (homework) question rather than just wasting everyone's time. Quora is not a effective place to answer homework. It's slow, and people will spot what you're doing and find a way to sabotage it. My suggestion is that instead you go ask a large language model such as chat GPT exactly this question, making sure you ask it to show it's working. LLMs are infamous for their hallucinations where they confidently report the wrong answer. They especially have trouble with symbol manipulation which is required for many things including arithmetic. That's why you add the cue around showing the steps. You don't need to be handed the answer on a plate because because being reminded of the steps makes the problem trivial. “To calculate the time it takes for #16,840 to earn #2,947 of simple interest at 5% per annum, you can use the formula for simple interest: \[Simple \ Interest = \frac{Principal \ (P) \times Rate \ (R) \times Time \ (T)}{100}\] …” (Remainder cut). The neat thing about this is it mirrors how people use computers in the real world. People forget little details but all they need is a scaffold to get going again. Oh and save Quora for questions that require human experience.

Question: It is so annoying to go through job interviews without a solid number for salary compensations. What stage should it be brought up or even right away maybe?

Question: Are there enough battery recharging facilities to recharge your Tesla electric car across the length and width of a country?
Answer: My parents live in a small town that serves the local farming community. It’s not ‘on the way’ to anywhere. As a consequence, the road to them is not exactly well populated. Your choice is either to detour via the motorway which over an hour, or to head direct and drive through small town after small town. I lost count of the number of chargers on the route. I’d guess maybe ten? Roughly one every 40–60 minutes. Now none of these chargers are official Tesla chargers which is a bit of a pain because the car doesn’t know about them so it doesn’t precondition the battery or plan the trip around them. Otherwise though, there’s more than enough choices of where to stop. Most towns have a single charger near a cafe or supermarket. The app will tell me whether it’s in use before I arrive, and if so then I can either wait ten minutes or carry on to the next town. This seems to be pretty much universal now, every small town wants people with EVs to stop so there’s always an option. There are Tesla chargers both where my parents live and where I live but I don’t go to them as a slow charger at home is far more convenient. There are exceptions still, if you want to go tramping in the middle of nowhere then you would need to plan your trip. Let’s say your tramp is a two or three hour drive into the middle of nowhere, plus the same on the return trip, and you’re right at the upper limit of the car’s range without recharging.

Question: I want to create a personal library with the best 1,000 books ever. Can you tell me the best books you've ever read?
Answer: We live in a world where public libraries will send you any book you care to read, as will online book stores such as Amazon. Further, eReaders give virtually instantaneous access to millions of books. Back when I was a kid, library interloan systems were clunky and discouraged, and book stores were small. Having a large library of books guaranteed that you could always find something interesting to read. I remember going q long way out of our way to get to specialist bookstores, and stocking up for years to come. At the time a large personal library was mainly for your own benefit. Also when I was a kid, it was standard for every family to have a music collection. Each purchase told a story and the combination expressed their eclectic taste. Nowadays that's rare, and it's more common to share Spotify playlists. The role of a personal book collection in 2023 is similar but a little different to the role of a personal music collection. It serves the same purpose of expressing your personal taste and focus. Houses don't have much space and using some for say Pratchett is a way of saying what is important and meaningful to you. Books can also be loaned to visitors and friends. We often have people come to stay that read one of our books while they're here. It's a social thing; you can talk about the book together afterwards. Some people like to show off. Put say Chaucer, “Gödel, Escher, Bach”, Hawking, “Anna Karenina”, “Finnegans Wake” and Asimov on your shelf and we'll, you create an impression of someone that likes to read books that require thought, or at least who is pretending that is the case. You can find lists of “The greatest 1,000 books of all time “ in various places in the internet. You can even buy collections of them since most are out of copyright. The trouble with doing this is that people will ask you questions and, having not read the books, you will look like an idiot. Get books the moment before you want to read them, and either return or donate them afterwards. Keep those that have a big personal effect on you, and that becomes your personal library. I'm exaggerated slightly, it's pretty standard to have a stack of books you are about to read. For example you might preorder your favourite author’s latest, keep books loaned by a friend and pick up books based on recommendations. What I'm trying to highlight is the role of a personal library is the opposite of what it was when I was a kid. It uses to be that you would collect books you'd like to get around to reading, whereas now it'd be odd to have books which you haven't read.

Question: Statistically speaking, to what extent does locking your car prevent it from being stolen?
Answer: Statistically, this is very hard to measure. You'd think it would be easy, since we have lots of data points, but failing to lock your car is so correlated with other things that you can't build a causative model. To do that you'd need to cause locking to randomly fail and track the results. Anecdotally it doesn't make much difference. The kind of people that know how to break into a car also know how to start it. Virtually every car has an immobaliser, and since bypassing that is harder than bypassing the lock…

Question: Hi. Any computer programmers out there? I have a specific question. I’m writing a story about an experienced programmer who has been out of work for four months. Would it be hard Tor him to find freelance programming gigs?
Answer: There's a lot of difference between a bad coder and a good coder. A good coder has virtually nonstop offers of work. A bad coder…. Well, not everyone is willing to pay for a good coder and so some companies compromise. Coders who work freelance have extensive networks to help them find the next gig (or a recruitment agent doing this). As a consequence they can finish a job Friday and often have another one on Monday. It's different for permanent employees who have often not bothered to maintain those connections and don't have an up to date CV. If they're made redundant then it can be very tough. It's completely different if they choose to move, where they'll be seen as attractive based on their current job. My point is that your story has someone without work. That person is either a permanent employee that stopped playing the game, or a contractor with some downside (eg ADHD). Either way, yes, IT loves popular people and shuns people that are struggling. Breaking back in after a hiatus is totally different to getting a better role. I think you'll need to work out why your programmer doesn't have a job. But yes, would you trust a critical project to a freelancer who can't land a gig? My bet is you wouldn't even if that person offered to work for half rate.

Question: How do I calculate effective rate of interest if I take a loan of Rs. 5 Lacs at a flat interest rate of 6% pa for 3 years?

Question: How do you get a 20,000% increment in your salary in the last 25 years?
Answer: We say that an increase in salary from $20,000 to $40,000 is fundamentally different to an increase from $120,000 to $140,000 and you really need to use percentages. This question highlights the need for two further rules: Percentages start to become unwieldy at 100%. A 20000% salary increase is close enough to multiplying salary by 200. With three numbers rather than five it's considerably easier to understand. The second rule is that any time period over about five years should be adjusted for inflation or else the reader is left trying to work out whether the percentage increase is meaningless. We know the normal range of salaries is say $20,000 to $200,000. There are people outside this at both extremes, but for practical purposes the point is that salary can only increase by 10x. Any more and you are talking about something with such an extreme that the insanely high or low salary is the interesting story rather than the change over time.

Question: When buying a computer, why in the 90s were CD-ROMs included as a package but not anymore?
Answer: Remember CDs were originally popular for music and their immediate replacement, DVDs, were popular for movies. You don't buy music or movies on physical media anymore because downloading is faster and easier. It's the same with CD drives. I remember a time in the early nineties when we used to rent a CD drive for the weekend along with some shareware discs. You'd get literally hundreds of diskettes worth of games on a single CD. I can't overstate how incredible that data density was. Even compared to early internet connections it was still a pretty good choice. Downloading in CD quality over a modem would take over a day, plus your phone line was tied up. Eventually though internet connections got so fast that you can download the contents of a CD faster than you can get a physical CD out of its case. The last holdout for optical discs was backups. I remember maybe 2010 or so when you could buy a stack of quality DVDs pretty cheaply and back up by swapping the discs out every four or so gigabytes. It was a hassle but the cost per gigabyte justified it. Then stuff like Dropbox came along with similar cost per gig and much less hassle.

Question: A trader had 48,000 in a bank. After 5 years, the money had amounted to 600,000. At what rate per annum was the bank paying simple interest?
Answer: This is a trick question. It’s tricking you into saying: “we don’t know the rate of interest since the change in the trader’s bank balance comes from trading rather than interest.” It’s true that we don’t know the rate of compound interest, but that wasn’t the question asked. The question was “… simple interest”, and we know rate of simple interest was: Zero. Banks shifted from paying simple to compound interest in about the sixties. People writing trick questions like to include a false clue (a red herring) so that students skimming the question respond to the clue rather than reading the question carefully. Note that I did a quick google search before answering this and it seems some banks still use simple interest for their savings accounts. If you happen to be reading this somewhere that doesn’t do compound interest, then you’ll have to go with the ‘we don’t know’ answer.

Question: If everybody in America switched to an electric vehicle tomorrow, and there were ample charging stations, would the grid be able to handle the load?

EV manufacturers were ramping up production as fast as they could to try and satisfy this demand. During this time, we didn't have too much trouble building charging stations at the rate one per ten thousand cars sold or whatever the actual ratio was. So yes, if everyone woke up tomorrow and said: “you know what, my next car witbe an EV”, we would be able to build charging stations for them before we could deliver the cars. The power usage by electric cars is relatively minor, at around 10kWh per day. It's also conveniently at a time that has historically been a lull in demand. That said, decades of underinvestment in the grid have left it prone to breaking, to the point that even a modest increase in demand could be too much. Since electricity use is clearly going up rather than down, and power plants take many years to build, there is an urgent need to build more now. EVs aren't the problem there much more than say electric toothbrushes, both are basically rounding errors in demand. Also both would be largely unaffected by the odd power cut since they both have enough battery to easily wait for power to come back on. That's not true of AC units, or the laser cutter I just bought at work. We need to build more power plants because otherwise we won't being unable to turn on the AC, manufacture, produce steel, or use LLMs … those things matter regardless of your political persuasion.

Question: Is there an AI bubble now?
Answer: I’m going to answer this in a roundabout way by looking at index funds and the dotcom boom. Obviously just my personal opinion, not financial advice, etc. During the 90s we went from the internet being something most people had never heard of to something widely expected to completely transform the world. A lot of fortunes were made as people bet big on the likes of pets dot com, or this funny online CD store called Amazon taking on the big music retailers. This was followed by the dotcom crash, where numerous overinflated startups were brought back to reality (along with a bunch of good companies). That was over twenty years ago. Looking back, the total market cap of those dotcom companies was about right. The revolution they promised has happened, and it’s been at least as big as they claimed. The poster child of the dotcom boom and crash is pets dot com. Now twenty five years later I subscribe to a pet food delivery service and don’t recall the last time I physically walked into a pet store. At the same time the individual stocks which succeeded back then have largely all failed in future years. I mean sure, we can easily spot the ones that didn’t, but let’s look at the NASDAQ from 1999: Amazon, eToys, Pets Dot Com, Qualcomm, BroadVision, Metricom, Ortel, VeriSign, Cisco. Let’s say though that you’d invested not in these specific stocks, but in an index fund covering all of them. You hadn’t believed in eToys specifically so much as the dotcom boom in general. You’d have done very well for yourself You might have worried a little when your index went from $8000 to $2000, but just twenty years later and you’re back to $12,000. The underlying fundamentals were good: ‘the internet will revolutionise business’. It did, though picking winners is really hard. That brings us to AI. Can you guess which AI technology company will dominate in 2043, because I certainly can’t. A couple years ago we might have said the biggest and best AI company is Palantir. Now we might say it’s OpenAI. I’m sure some people will guess right and make a crazy amount of money. My bet though is that most will go the way of pets dot com and crash to almost nothing. Will NVidia still be the chipmaker of choice in 2048? Actually I’d go further and hypothesise that so many will crash to nothing we will have an AI bust, a bit like the dotcom bust. Fundamentally though AI will deliver on its promise: ‘People using this tech will do far better’ A bubble is when people invest only because they know another investor will buy it off them for more. What I think we have now is that technology has completely changed how we’re going to do business, nobody knows who the new set of winners will be, and so there’s a lot of guessing going on. I don’t think it’s a bubble because I think the total market cap attributed to AI is about right… I think a better term would be ‘an extremely volatile market’. I would expect that even an index fund of AI companies will be a very bumpy ride.

Question: Why can't every single parking lot in the car park be an EV charging point, so that drivers will not have to fuss about people hogging it after it’s done charging?
Answer: I can see this making sense for the kinds of lots that people use overnight. The average car drives 13,000 miles a year. However about a third of those are on long trips where people would use fast chargers regardless. That gives 10,000/year or 30/day. That takes about 10kWh or $2/day. That's not really enough to need precise billing. It's ‘close enough’ to add perhaps ten dollars a week to the cost of renting a park and skip billing entirety. This also means the total draw of the lot is manageable. You've got say ten hours to add 10kWh to each car. A power draw up to 250kWh is possible without too much infrastructure, so a lot can recharge 250 cars overnight with commonly available infrastructure. Malls and the like are a different story. I don't see there ever being significant demand.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: I'm doing organic marketing letting people know that I offer makeup services. I have a problem with converting them into a booked client. What's your advice on converting someone into a booked client?
Answer: Talk to them, ask them rather than us. Three possible reasons: They would never book. They are not right for your service. You're wasting your time trying to get them in. They don't live anywhere near you. They might be interested, but email goes much further than a car. Going straight from a passive email to in person booking is too much. You need an intermediate step. Don't guess, get in contact with a dozen or two until you can roughly put percentages into each bucket (or a bucket I missed). The strategies for each are completely different, so there is almost nothing you can do without more information. Plus this step is free, and always good practice.

Question: How many miles does one hour of charging produce for the Tesla Model 3?
Answer: A supercharger can fill roughly half the battery in fifteen minutes. The last little bit of charge (95% to 100%) takes a long time and I can imagine going from 0% to 100% taking a full hour, but that's not how you're supposed to use it. If you're going on a long drive then you stop when you're below about 20% and charge it up to say 70% which should take as little as fifteen minutes. So a long trip that includes an hour of charging should have roughly filled the battery twice over, essentially giving you three times your starting range.

Question: Is a $339 USD toothbrush really needed for proper teeth health?
Answer: No. My wife picked researching the effectiveness of electric toothbrushes for her undergraduate project and I got to review the stats. Everything about these fancier bricks is designed to make it easier to do a good job: oscillating head, 3D tracking, timer, pressure sensor, Bluetooth. For example Bluetooth answers how often you forget to brush. The killer chart for me was a study of twenty people where half were given a manual brush and the rest a fairly fancy electric one. Treatment was training on proper brushing. Results were clear: there was no significant difference between the two groups after treatment but there was before treatment with the electric toothbrushes winning.

Question: Why would someone pay the extra cost for a Macbook if they could get a Windows laptop with equivalent hardware for much less? I really want to understand, why would a standard user choose Apple ever? Your ego aside, please.
Answer: The place where a windows computer saves money is in having more choices so you can pick your compromises. For example my main work computer is what's affectionately known as a luggable. It's technically portable but both too heavy and too little battery life to use for more than an hour away from a desk. It cost around $1500. The only apple with equivalent power is the MacBook Pro 16″. For $3099 you can get that with the same storage and almost as much RAM (32 vs 40 GB). You're literally paying double. That Mac is a far better machine. Rather than a luggable, it weighs just four pounds and has a twenty hour battery life. Why would you choose the Mac? Because you don't want to compromise. Lousy battery life and heavy, or double the price. Or… notably inferior specs for the same price. Some people are willing to pay for things done properly. Others prefer to save by taking shortcuts.

Question: How many of you were in debt in your 20s and what did you do to be more financially comfortable after your 20s?
Answer: I had student loan debt throughout my 20s but that was it. Mostly I earned some money tutoring, and then spent down to roughly zero by the next pay period. I needed to get better at budgeting for that transition, as previously I would simply spend nothing when things screwed up, but now with monthly, quarterly and annual bills I couldn't get away with spending nothing.

Question: Being a housewife sounds like a good deal to me because your husband's income is your income, and the workplace is a war-zone. Why do feminists call it patriarchal oppression?
Answer: When my wife went back to work I noticed we had a drop in quality of life. All those little things she'd been doing around the house generated more joy than we could get from the extra income and I encouraged her to stay at home. She didn't for two reasons: Firstly she enjoyed the work better. It was much harder mentally required attention to detail in a way that running a house does not. Secondly she was worried about her independence. If we got divorced or I was unable to work then the labour market for long term housewives is poor. As for why it's called patriarchal oppression, that relates to both points above. I would prefer she stayed home because that would make my life easier - her preference doesn't register. The second one is more about control - if she's dependent on my income then I could demand she does things and her choices would be comply or be out on the streets. If she's independent then she'd simply tell me to shove it. Earning the money means I'm in a position to control the money.

Question: Why has the news been blocked about the government trying to figure out how to tax electric cars?
Answer: The news hasn’t been blocked. Governments are always thinking about how to adjust the tax system as technology changes things. You can read proposals on how the government might change tax based on AI, wealth, capital gains, blockchain, … For example if business becomes more efficient through the use of generative AI then it can produce just as much with fewer workers. That means increased unemployment but more money to pay for it. What’s the right way to handle that? The increasing use of digital currency means that people can buy and sell goods and services without ‘money’ changing hands, skipping both sales and income tax. The increasing use of EVs means fuel tax is pretty useless and if you want to encourage lighter EVs to reduce road maintenance then you might want to charge more for heavier vehicles. All of this is fully public. It’s not on the news because most people find discussions of tax optimisation to be incredibly boring. But if it floats your boat then you’re in luck - the proliferation of the internet means you can listen to specialist podcasts or blogs without worrying that it isn’t covered by the mainstream press.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: How do you feel about a tax system which taxes only land owned? It is a flat tax. It will tax it in perpetuity and the only way to free yourself of the tax is to sell the land.
Answer: The first thing that I always think about when someone proposes changing the tax system is… how will this be abused. Always remember the anecdote about English manors without windows due to the tax. In this case two obvious things spring to mind. Rich people can suppress their desire to own a big house and live somewhere modest, essentially avoiding tax. Secondly, food needs space to grow and high density farming is not good for the soil. This will push up the cost of food. Most likely this tax only applies to this country, so everyone will abandon farming and import all food. You better hope the supply chain never breaks. Two suggestions: firstly, rather than inventing a new system and working out why it doesn't work, instead work out what you don't like about the current system and make a small tweak. For example taxing income rather than wealth strongly encourages hiding income. Decreasing income tax and introducing a wealth tax addresses that. Secondly there are a lot of things where everyone knows it would be better, but nobody knows how to make the change. The metric system, universal healthcare, etc. Focus on a concrete change that could be introduced now. Perhaps a register of assets. Something that even incompetent governments will achieve.

Question: Does anyone ever prefer to work two part time jobs instead of one full time job, not because they have to, but so that they can work in two different fields and have a more flexible resume? Is it ever advisable to do this?
Answer: I kinda do this. As a consultant I work across multiple clients and industries. Those clients pretty universally want 100% of my attention for the duration of the engagement. I've had to push pretty hard to get part-time. I've found a number of benefits though. Firstly it really helps my sanity. Every workplace has a bunch of good stuff and dumb stuff. I find if I stick to one place then the good stuff becomes expected while the dumb stuff becomes increasingly obvious. Moving between the two really helps to keep perspective. Secondly it helps with my income security. Clients end contracts for all sorts of reasons and going from charging to not is never fun. Because I effectively get half my income from each, I don't ever go down to zero. This also helps with contract negotiations since I can afford to walk away. There's lots of downsides too, but I find that it's slightly better overall intend to keep doing it.

Question: If only 14% of Americans had a home computer in 1995, does that mean most people would go to the library if they needed computer access? Could you access chat rooms on a library computer?
Answer: The internet was still not such a big thing in 1995, most people with a computer did not go online. If you went and used a computer at the library then it was either to search the catalog or to look things up in the shiny new digital encyclopedia ‘encarta’. Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: I just started a tech company that would focus more on technological innovation. What are some tips on how to make my company a success?
Answer: Work out how you're going to make money. Start with visualising the money turning up in your bank account and work backwards. Make sure your plan includes more money coming in than out. I'll Illustrate with an example of where I failed to do this. About ten years ago, CME was scaling from being an awesome customer engagement platform for one client to supporting multiple clients. The system needed to identify how interested each customer was in every message we could send, and I felt that being by far the best in the world at this would be out competitive edge. We implemented deep learning from scratch, reading research papers and translating it into code. It was a monumental amount of work and we went head to head with Google on tech when they released tensorflow. It was pretty awesome for a startup with eight people. I even looked at buying one if the first commercial quantum computers to help with the simulated annealing. That's how I saw it. Now let's look from the perspective of one of our clients. They were using the software with a somewhat antique interface (pre-web). It had only basic asset management and the strong focus on ‘segment-of-one’ meant setting up a simple message was a lot of steps. Now in addition to eligibility criteria, the system was scoring messages so audience counts were jumping all over the place. Compared to the old method where every message had a propensity model, this new one was just that much more complicated. Users tolerated it. Maybe they even liked being on the bleeding edge, or just liked our enthusiasm. Anyway we earned maybe $5,000 a month from extra sales due to the smarter message selection. Clients got slightly better messages/ products in front of customers and sold a little more so it was probably fair. The trouble is we'd invested several hundred thousand dollars in developing the tech and were spending around $10k/month maintaining it. This technology innovation was cool, but monetizing it by adding it to an existing product with just five clients? It's painfully obvious that won't ever cover costs. You need scale to benefit from innovation and we didn't have scale. If we'd owned SFMC with many thousands of clients. Coming back to you… I'm sure you know that nobody buys ideas, they buy execution. Equally, nobody buys technological innovation. You need to apply that innovation in the market at scale yourself.

Question: My car, a Toyota Avensis 2010, is making 9.3km/l. Is this a good economy?
Answer: We had a similar car and worked out we were spending so much on fuel that we could replace it with a brand new fuel-efficient car and save money. The arithmetic is pretty simple. 9.3L/100km vs a hybrid at say 3.3L/100km saves 6L. How much is six litres of fuel where you live? How many 100km do you drive per year? We did this back when hybrids were pretty new and not yet widely available on the secondhand market, a bit like the situation with EVs now. You can make the numbers work much better by getting a three or so year old fuel efficient car. Some people do the calculation and use it to justify getting a new EV. That works, but only if you ignore that a three year old car would score better.

Question: Why aren't electric vehicle batteries easily swapped for a fully charged one? They could be in a separate standard trailer. You stop and just swap batteries instead of waiting to charge.
Answer: Sounds good in theory, been tried, didn't get market traction. One downside of this idea is that for every car sold you will have to build more than one battery. That's a massive amount of depreciation which will have to be passed on. Would you rather spend $200/month on your car payment, or $250/month on your battery lease. You'll also lose innovation as all battery packs will have to be standardized, and lose range as you need to increase insulation. Otherwise there is a lot of appeal to this. The tech is relatively easy. First you save heaps on the purchase price, and second refilling the battery is as simple as driving up to a robotic swap unit.

Question: If Jeff Bezos and Elon Musk evenly distributed all their wealth, what would be the effects?
Answer: Bezos and Musk are rich but they’re not rich enough that redistributing their wealth would make a material difference to the average American. Bezos is estimated to be worth $150B and Musk $250B for a combined $400B but a lot of that is tied up in Amazon and Tesla respectively. Realistically what we’re taking about is everyone being given a tiny share in these big companies. The population of America is 340m so in round numbers you’re talking about giving every American $1,000. We’re talking the same order of magnitude as the covid stimulus checks. As for the effect, it is mildly inflationary. It helps your standard B2C businesses, especially the discretionary ones, as people go ahead with a few purchases that they previously would have deferred. Walmart would probably be the biggest winner. Far more interesting would be trying to guess what happens to Amazon and Tesla. Without a single large shareholder having an outsized influence in the company’s direction, I would expect both to turn into more regular large corporates. My gut reaction is that will cause Amazon to very slowly fade away, while it might actually help Tesla. I can’t think of any similar experiment we could use as a baseline.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: If someone invented the cure for cancer, how wealthy would they become compared to Elon Musk or Jeff Bezos?
Answer: Let’s pretend that despite the legions of past research into cancer by innumerable brilliant people, it turns out that a simple magic pill is able to cure cancer by flagging cancerous cells for recycling. Let’s assume that this is dead-end research, the magic pill is perfect so cancer is such a perfect fit that cancer is no longer an issue but the whole approach cannot be applied to anything else. I’ve created this scenario because most major advances have knock on effects that can be as big as the initial achievement. For example nanobots that rush around your body curing cancer could also rush around your body doing infinite other useful things. One in six people die of cancer. The total worldwide pharmaceutical spend on all drugs is $1.5T, so I’m going to estimate $250m as the market opportunity. By comparison the current pharmaceutical spend is $150m, so I’m assuming this will almost double due to the new treatment being so much better. However almost none of this revenue goes to the scientist that makes the breakthrough. My guess is they’ll make their employer obscenely wealthy, and that employer will give them a bonus in the tens of millions of dollars as a way to say thank you and encourage future staff to dream big.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: Why do marriages in the past endure the test of time, but today marriages end up in break-ups despite the increase in education and civilization?
Answer: I’ll use an example from the parents of a friend of mine who were born in the 30s. They got married when she was 20 which was pretty normal in the 50s. She had worked a few jobs since leaving school at 16 but of course she had to stop the moment she was married. A couple of kids later and her job was obviously to ‘make home’. As a cabinetmaker he never had a lot of money but it was enough for an honest working-class life. The marriage was certainly not happy at this point, but well, they got by. A curveball was thrown when their daughter had a baby at 16, which they adopted - but I’m not sure it really changed the outcome. The husband retired about the point the youngest child left home. The parents hadn’t liked each other for a long time, but they’d tolerated each other’s company and well, they hadn’t needed to see a lot of each other. After this point though they were both at home full time and could no longer escape each other’s company. The trouble was they had no money - she simply couldn’t leave because even though she hated his guts by this point, she hadn’t worked in thirty odd years. They were just scraping by financially because they had two pensions and only one house. There’s absolutely no way she could have afforded even a modest rent. So they stayed married for over fifty years until he finally died. She’d raised the three children, and he’d provided what he could in terms of money and discipline. “… despite the increase in education and civilization” Have a look back over the anecdote above. Had she been better educated then she would have been able to get a job. Increases in civilization would also have provided her with more support if she’d left. Without either of those things, she had no option except to stay in a miserable marriage.

Question: Why is there a female to male wage gap for the same job?
Answer: The short answer is there isn't. The wave gap comes up when comparing different jobs (eg labourer vs childcare worker). It also comes up in a large company when you look at who gets promoted. I had a friend that did a detailed statistical analysis of pay for a large organisation looking for bias. It's extremely hard to measure just the effect of gender, for example women tend to work slightly fewer hours per week in salaried roles, and working longer hours is associated with getting bigger raises. Also men are, on average, more likely to ask for raises during annual reviews. Women are paid less for equivalent work (same level of qualification and experience), but they are paid roughly the same if they are doing the same work.

Question: Why do you have to choose a good company?
Answer: I'll give an anecdote related to pa, but before I begin, I want to emphasise that this applies across the board. It's less important with pay than other things, that's just the only example I can give from first-hand experience. Imagine the same job at two companies. Where would you like to work?

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: Is community college a waste of time for pathetic people who don’t have money to attend university?
Answer: I grew up with a bit of predujice about community college. Perhaps a little different to yours in that money was never part of it, but just as bad. After my wife graduated from uni, she found a job in a small town, too small to have a university and so I found myself a job teaching at the local community college. That was a massive eye opener for me, neither the teaching staff or the students were anything like I'd imagined. The teaching staff were awesome, most were former school teachers, and many were active in what's now called the maker community. Yes, they weren't publishing international research on ray tracing, neural models of sleep, constrained sorting or the like. Instead their focus was more on student achievement. They were also publishing their findings on the effectiveness of different teaching techniques. I don't know if you've been to uni, but the standard of teaching is well pretty poor. The staff are all professional researchers and they've been asked to squeeze in some teaching despite minimal training. Kinda like grabbing the best mechanics you can find and telling them they're to teach a class on car repair. Results were highly variable. The students were also anything but lazy. Most had left school, got a job and realised that path would not give them a good career. My class had mums juggling education and childcare, people working full time, an athlete trying to build skills while competing, and numerous people that had got a job as a dockworker and were now completely retraining. My point is that none of them were slackers. They were there to learn and get a good job, not because their parents told them to go to uni so they did. Yes they were not academically gifted, but they sure made up for it with proper time management and hard work. I'm telling this story because it was a crazy confluence of factors that led to me being there. Most people in my position would have gone through their whole life without having that prejudice challenged. I was wrong about community college, so how many other things am I also wrong about? That experience has made me very cynical of people, especially reporters and politicians, talking about things where they have no first-hand experience.

Question: Why is Mark Zuckerberg copying Elon Musk?

Question: What are the most effective ways to save money on a tight budget while living in one of the most expensive cities on Earth?

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: Will electric cars - due to their significantly increased weight due to their batteries - cause more potholes to appear on our roads? Wear goes up as the fourth power of weight.
Answer: The fourth power of weight? That’s incredible! A semi weighs 80,000 pounds, while a car weighs 3,000 pounds - The semi is 25 times the weight. So, since we’re working in the fourth power for pothole development, that means a single truck will generate 25^4 times more potholes than a single car. That’s 400,000 times as many potholes. So one truck doing a single truck causes as much damage as almost half a million cars. Since our roads seem to survive this, a few slightly heavier cars are not going to cause them much trouble.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: Are 1,000 mile car batteries a game changer for EVs?
Answer: Remember each mile of range is another pound of batteries to carry on every trip, and the smart money is on not taking on more weight than you need. Let’s say 95% of your trips are under 300 miles, would you rather have a car that’s tuned for that 95%, or one that’s tuned for the 5%. There’s two obvious exceptions: Firstly the road warriors proud of their long trips without stopping. I had an all-day meeting about 100 miles from home. That’s fine because my car can drive 200 miles without charging. But if that meeting had been 200 miles away then I’d have been late getting home because I’d have to stop and charge. That would’ve sucked - I don’t want to stop and charge on a two to three hour trip! Do that with any regularity and you can bet I’d buy a 500 mile car. Secondly the people who park somewhere without electricity such as the side of the road. They might only be able to charge up conveniently say once a week, so they really need plenty of range for the full week. Lots of parking garages are currently not set up for EVs and I’m sure building owners are trying to put off expensive retrofits. One thousand mile batteries will be a game changer for both those groups. You’ll find the rest of us are much more interested in getting the same range at lower cost/weight. Having a thousand mile range appeals about as much as putting a spare fuel tank in your trunk.

Question: I put in my 2 weeks resignation notice a week ago and my manager is assigning me so much work during my last 3 days. How do I address my concerns?
Answer: Any advice you read on the internet about leaving a job will tell you to avoid burning bridges. You’ll be remembered more by your behaviour during these two weeks than anything up until this point. What these people remember about you will matter: perhaps the new job doesn’t work out and you need a reference from them? Perhaps one of them becomes a key client to your new role? I start with that preface because it’s now the most important thing, and so working out how to handle unreasonable requests, you should view that through the prism of leaving a good impression. One option is of course to work your ass off. Do sixteen hour days for the remainder of the notice period. Will that leave a good impression? Perhaps it will annoy them that you didn’t work that hard during the rest of your time there. Personally I’d go for having a cordial conversation with your manager. Something like “Boss, what you’ve asked me to do in the next three days is more than I can get through. Would you like to sort the tasks by priority, or are you comfortable with me judging their priority?” The impression this leaves is someone that’s aware of their own limitations and is deliberate about working within them. It also avoids you arriving at your new job feeling frazzled. Mostly I’ve seen this come up because the manager has screwed up for a long time. For example a friend of mine resigned recently after complaining about being overloaded for months. Suddenly the manager realised that would leave an in-progress project and desperately pushed him to hit a logical milestone. He’s been cheery and helpful, and he’s also been stopping on the dot of five.

Question: What's the difference between Indigent Care and Universal Health Care?
Answer: Indigent care is a little like food stamps. Some members of the public are able to shop in a private business for free. They’re only allowed to purchase certain products - couldn’t have them using food stamps to buy condoms after all… Universal health care is a little like voting. The government runs it and pays for it, not the people using the service. Sometimes the service is better in some areas than others, and sometimes the service really isn’t good enough. Universal health care covers all citizens, just like all citizens are eligible to vote. Rich or poor, young or old. Universal health care covers most medical treatments: cancer, dialysis, MRIs, etc. If your healthcare professional says you need it then it’s covered. By contrast Indigent care only covers the poor, only covers some services: “Benefits are limited to participating administrators who provide primary, preventative and some specialty services”. Earn a lot of money but are transferring between jobs so don’t have healthcare for a few days? You’d be covered under universal healthcare but not under Indigent care. Broke your leg for the fifteenth time because you won’t give up dangerous sports? You’d be covered under universal healthcare. Really, really want a CT scan but your doctor says no? You can’t get one under universal healthcare - the medical profession prioritises who gets treatment.

Question: How can we make health care available for everyone? Is there a country that has better health care than in the U.S.?

If that problem is your health, and you (or your insurance) have the money available, then there are no real limits on the treatment available. Question: How is employee engagement really important, or is it just a new buzz phrase?
Answer: Why are so many questions written in the either/or format when the answer is never just one option? Employee engagement is critical; think about how productive you are when you really believe in the importance of your work and contrast that with how productive you are when you’re being paid by the hour, you hate your job, your boss doesn’t understand what you do and simply needs to see your seat being kept warm. The difference is so huge it’s hard to articulate. Perhaps similar to how productive you are when you’ve got a particularly nasty virus versus when you’re feeling awesome. Even just a tiny increase to employee engagement makes a massive difference to productivity. As per the standard quote: Culture eats strategy for breakfast. And yet, when most companies talk about employee engagement they’re normally talking about some new HR system designed to increase engagement. Just like customer engagement platforms before them, employee engagement systems rarely increase employee engagement. What’s the first thing that comes to mind for you when you think about a “employee engagement system”? For me it’s those weird corporate events where you do team building, the ‘shout outs’ during meetings. These don’t increase employee engagement in any meaningful way. I’d describe it as giving the company a facade of having engaged employees. So when I hear about how a company is going to focus on employee engagement, the first thing that comes to mind for me is cynicism. Employee engagement is absolutely critical, and it’s mostly used as a buzzword. Do the staff absolutely love their jobs - they’re working there because they’re passionate about it and the difference they’re making? Are you paying them because otherwise they’d have to go get a job to support themselves and their family, but if they were independently wealthy then they’d keep doing this? That’s employee engagement. Everyone needs money: You need a roof over your head, food on your table, and clothes on your back. Most people would earn about the same money if they changed jobs, so saying they’re going to work for the money is technically true but misses the point. Why are they going to this job rather than another one that pays the same. As an employer you need to meet the market rate for the job, and pretty much everything else you do beyond that will impact employee engagement one way or another. How interesting is the work? How much difference does they get to make? Are their colleagues fun to be around? Are there silly rules that make them feel like a child? Is the company rewarding slackers or is everyone working equally hard? Is the company underpaying slightly ‘because it’s a great place to work’? Employee engagement is the reason you go to work besides money and it is both the most important determiner of a company’s success and a meaningless buzzword.

Question: Do owners of electric cars get excited when there is free charging available?
Answer: No. It costs me an order of magnitude more to charge using a commercial charger rather than at home where it's essentially free. Charging at home is also far more convenient: I plug in, sleep for the night, and the car is full the next morning. I don't care whether recharging took one hour or ten. As a consequence I almost never charge away from home. It happens maybe once or twice a quarter. I'm also not doing full charges away from home, because lbreakfast or unch only takes so long. It's a little top up. Whether that top up is free or charged at a hefty premium makes a big price difference in the moment, but very little difference to my monthly budget. It's like chilli paste. It should really be free since it's so cheap to produce, but even if it's sold at an outrageous profit, it just won't make any real difference. Still, I dislike paying a premium. Last time I was away for the weekend there were two charges in town: one was free at one restaurant complex, while the other was full price. I went with the free option.

Question: Do Teslas learn specific roads? If previous Teslas have swerved to avoid a pothole, will other Teslas be aware of it?

There is the ability for the cars to learn, but it's much more controlled than that. For example Tesla might observe that they have a lot of complaints about cars mishandling potholes, so they put software on the cars to monitor them and send back pothole footage. Then Tesla train their software using that footage and send out an update.

Question: You have a choice between two EVs. They are the same size and have the same specs except one has a range of 150 mile and costs $20k. The other has a range of 280 miles and costs $35k. Which would you purchase if you had to choose?

I also have the choice of waiting a few more months when many more EVs will be available. Your question pretty much is “Should I buy a Nissan Leaf or a BYD Atto 3”. There are people for whom the Leaf is the better choice, people for whom the BYD is better, and many people that wouldn’t be happy with either. In my personal case, I drive over 150 miles every month or two. I’d now have to swap cars with my wife for those trips which would be annoying but we’d manage. I almost never drive over 280 miles, and I’m happy to stop and charge mid-journey for something that rare. So if there was nothing different about the cars then I’d go for the cheaper one. It serves my day-to-day needs, and a once every month-or-two hassle isn’t worth an extra $15k. In the real world though, the BYD has far more boot space than the Leaf. It’s got more height and is generally more comfortable to drive. If I was choosing between the BYD for $35k and the Leaf for $20k, I’d go for the BYD because I take the dogs to the park every week and that’d be a pain in the Leaf.

Question: How can I know which stocks I should invest in?
Answer: here’s only been twice in my life where I was certain what stocks to invest in, and both were frauds where I was an expert in the field and could see through it. That’s over twenty years. Note that even if you know for sure that something is a fraud, to make money you still need enough that the broker doesn’t force your hand before the market catches up with you. The reason it’s hard is that every stock is owned by someone that’s done their homework and believes that stock is worth more. Every stock for sale is someone that’s done their homework and believes the stock will drop. There might be a lot of investors that haven’t done very much homework, but they are all pretty small time. The investors you end up betting against are all professionals that study this stuff all day, every day. To me, that gives two options: stick to private companies that the professionals can’t touch, and/or invest using a formula. Something like an index fund means that rather than picking a stock, you instead by a tiny slice of every single stock in the market and therefore are all-but guaranteed to get the market average performance.

Question: In all seriousness, just how easy/difficult is it to bribe a judge? Is it more likely that they'll just accept the bribe and judge you accordingly anyway? Say if someone decide to try to bribe a judge with 10 million US Dollars, would it work?
Answer: I am not familiar with judges, but I am familiar with a few other bribery scandals. Two main things: Firstly there is nothing so crude as a transfer of money. It's things like being invited on exclusive conferences, you or family members getting unrelated jobs or contracts. There is no 'because you did this, I'll do that’. More, spending time together and listening to their point of view. Even if you were somehow able to record every interaction, you won't find a smoking gun. Secondly everyone knows and more importantly trusts one another. You are receiving favours from your college buddy you've known for decades, and people introduced to you through this trusted connection. Basically don't think of it like bribery in the movies, but more like lobbying of politicians. That brings me to another point, it's often legal or at least not obviously illegal. The close contact let's you understand what they're thinking. At least, that's how the business ones operated before they blew up. I'm assuming judge's are similar.

Question: If you were about to start your dream career at 29 with no kids, less than $5000 in debt, and a tax free salary of $140,000 CDN: what would you do to become financially successful long term? (Will be starting a 4 year contract, looking for advice)

If you cook, do your own maintenance, and don't need much space, then you'll have more than enough money at a much lower income. Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: Is there ever a point to "debtor's prison" if it just prohibits people from paying off debts?
Answer: The purpose of debtors prisons was to terrify debtors into making sure they paid their bills. Take myself. I borrowed money to start a business. Before borrowing that money I looked at my likely reward (i.e. how much money I expected to make), and what risks I was taking on. For me the consequences of failure were that I’d lose my family home as well as all other savings. Then I’d basically be let go, I wouldn’t lose my job, I wouldn’t serve time in prison, that’d be it. Imagine if instead the consequences were that I’d be put in chains and paraded around. That I’d work in indentured servitude to the bank for the rest of my life. I wouldn’t have dared start the business, which means that the bank’s money was safe against me borrowing and then losing it. So the point in debtors prison was not really to get people to pay off debts, it was to terrify them away from taking on a debt that they might be unable to repay. As a consequence, money lenders and money borrowers were supposed to feel comfortable trading at low rates since lenders were very confident in being repaid.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: What are some tips to manage personal finance better?
Answer: The big thing for me was a mindset shift. I’d always viewed budgeting as spending less and depriving myself. A bit like ‘eat your greens’, I’d viewed it as spending on the things I should be buying at the expense of things that I wanted to buy. The shift was to eliminate savings, and instead budget on spending money in the future. Now I wasn’t choosing between ‘saving’ vs ‘grabbing some quick food on the way home so I don’t have to cook’ , but instead between ‘going on a winter holiday’ vs ‘grabbing some quick food on the way home so I don’t have to cook’. This is big, because it means the purpose of spending money is now to enjoy myself, to “create beautiful memories”… I’m deliberately not spending on that quick meal because I think I’ll get more out of something else.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: How do I save $1k+ per year (while earning minimum wage)?

You can save virtually every dollar you earn, with just a few small expenses (health insurance, clothes, etc). This is actually quite common - for example farm hands. My wife used to work when the kids were young and we employed a live-in au-pair. She ended up earning about the same as my wife, but we didn’t really have a choice as taking years off would have affected my wife’s career too much. Anyway, the au-pair ended up being able to spend thousands on fun tourist holidays because she hadn’t had any expenses. You can also save if you can get free rent (e.g. house sitting, or staying in a friend’s spare room or couch). That’s much harder as food will use most of your income, but $1k/year is still possible.

Question: How will the staff on a three star Michelin restaurant act if you let them know you don't drink wine?

Question: I had a nice job once and I was using the money to build a house but now I am out of job and I want to sell the unfinished house to start a business. Am I making the right decision?

Question: How important is having a standardized electric vehicle charging system for the future of EVs?

Question: Is it wrong for me, a 16-year-old guy, to go after a 19 (almost 20) year old girl that I feel really strongly about?

Question: Is it good or bad to date a 39-year-old while I'm 54?

Question: Is an electric car worth it if you don't drive much?
Answer: If you don’t drive much then your primary cost is depreciation. You basically want the cheapest car you feel safe in and isn’t too expensive to service. Most likely that’s a ten year old old ICE vehicle. Whatever was particularly popular where you lived about ten years ago. Being popular will also make servicing cheaper and easier. As of 2023, that’s unlikely to be an EV. I’d say you’re a good ten years away from them being more ubiquitous on the secondhand market than ICE vehicles.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: Do you think electric cars are the future? Do you prefer them over conventional cars?
Answer: Electric cars have already won. I’d highlight that even the alternatives we see such as hydrogen and PHEV cars are regular battery electric cars plus a way of recharging the battery. There is no significant innovation happening with internal combustion, every single manufacturer from Tesla to Tata to Toyota is going all-in on electric motors. The only open question is whether significant onboard battery capacity will win, or a method to recharge the more modest battery. Personally I have no skin in the game and don’t really care what the outcome is. I have a current car (BEV) and because I think that’s the most practical technology for me right now. I have the luxury of being able to recharge at home. If someone makes something better before I buy my next car then I’ll get that instead. I’m not holding my breath: using hydrogen for example requires astronomical amounts of cheap energy (probably nuclear fusion is the only practical way to get enough), some sort of awesome distribution network, and some way to make hydrogen vehicles safer than BEVs in a collision. That’s three massive hurdles.

Question: I'd rather have 5 million dollars than 1 billion because 5 is more than 1. Do you agree?

Question: What percentage of your wealth should be spent when buying a car in cash?
Answer: The phrasing of this question is really weird. If you spend more than you earn then you'll quickly end up broke no matter how much you start with. Let me try and give a more realistic example: Gen is a solo mom. She finally dumped her boyfriend after he would never contribute fairly to household chores. Fortunately she has a $2m trust fund to live off. Gen decides she needs a new car to get her kids to daycare, do the shopping and go to dance class. Being the analytical sort, she works out she spends five hours a week in the car out of 112 awake hours and so the car should get about five percent of her income. With two million in her trust fund she will get a stipend of $80k per year. From this she first has to pay tax and health insurance 1/3 which leaves her $53k. Five percent of that is $2650 but note this also has to cover car insurance and maintenance so leaving maybe $1500/year. Gen can therefore afford a $7500 car every five years. She pays cash of course, and it happens to be about 0.25% of her wealth.

Question: If you're not spending any money on advertising, etc., how much can you really make with online businesses?
Answer: Tesla has a total revenue of around $25B. Without an advertising budget you need to create awareness of your product through some other method.
