Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: Why is Toyota not enthusiastic about the transition from fossil fuel vehicles to electric vehicles?
Answer: Toyota was very early to EVs with the release of the Prius hybrid in 1997. That was wildly successful and Toyota was sitting pretty until Tesla came along. Furthermore it wasn’t until very recently that the majority of people realised EVs were going to take over; you have had fans of Tesla since the start but for a long time they were outnumbered by detractors, who pointed out (correctly) that Tesla only produced luxury vehicles in tiny quantities. Imagine you’re in the boardroom of Toyota. Your company dominates many segments including the key consumer segments with your hybrids. This funny EV startup who doesn’t even use dealers is gaining a lot of momentum, but they’re still selling as many cars a year as you sell in a good week. Is it really so surprising that Toyota bet on the trend fading like so many previous trends? It was far too late for Toyota once EVs got enough momentum that it’s painfully obvious they’re going to be the future. Changing their supply chain to make EVs cheaply will require almost reinventing the company, and they’ll be literally years behind most competitors. At this point they’ve got two choices: become a minor player, or bet everyone else is wrong and hope to get lucky. Again, I can understand them taking that risk. Maybe nuclear fusion will become commercially viable in the next five years, at which point hydrogen fuel cells or similar become the logical choice. Maybe they’ll surprise everyone with a crazy-fast transition. Maybe there will be enough people left that can’t charge overnight to keep things going. To me it sure looks like another Kodak moment.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: Why do bars and restaurants lose money?
Answer: Rent is brutal; bars and restaurants need to be in popular areas with good frontage. Do something wrong so your patron numbers drop off and the rent will put you straight into the red. Look at a random bar and take a guess what the lease is per week. If you’re more used to residential property then perhaps imagine getting a penthouse apartment in this location and of this size. Now let’s assume the gross profit per drink sold is $2 or so, how many drinks will you need to sell per week to cover that lease? Realistically most bars only have a couple busy nights a week so don’t judge them by sales during peak times. This is why you sometimes get weird restaurants clinging on in out-of-the-way locations. If they own the building or are operating somewhere with modest rent then there’s much less commercial pressure on them. They might not run at a profit but they also don’t cost money. This is especially true where staffing is flexible, such as a bar at a conference, which can simply redirect regular staff to the bar when they want to open.

Question: Would you post your property for sale on a new property listing website for free or pay for costly advertisement on an established website?

Question: Is saving in a bank a safe way to earn money with an interest rate of 8-10%, but if you are willing to risk a little you can, the interest rate can be up to 50-100% with RBIF?

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: If we have a billionaire father who puts 10 million dollars in an interest-bearing account when they are born for his kids and he will give it to them at 21. How much money would be in the account? 10 million 21 years later?
Answer: Assuming this is an arithmetic question, you can calculate 1.03^21 and get a number like an 86% increase. In real terms, regular interest-bearing savings accounts traditionally track below the rate of inflation so the young adult will have less than $10m in today’s money. Note that this is crazy-unrealistic, as a billionaire, the father would not be managing his finances directly. He’d have started with his accountant, and that person would have worked with his lawyer and the bank to set up something sensible. That might involve creating a trust for the kid rather than simply an account in their name, so that if the trustee can choose to withhold the money if appropriate. It might not too - for large amounts of money it’s worth being aware of the laws and structuring things appropriately. The $10m investment is much more likely to involve shares than a savings account. Even if it does involve cash, term investments give a better return than high-yield savings accounts. Then you have to subtract tax, inflaton, and the fees charged for managing the money.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: How much money do I need to make a month to buy a $90k house?
Answer: There thing this is missing is that location determines price. Back when my wife and I were looking for our first home we felt the market was really expensive but that we could just push ourselves to $350k. For that we could either get something ok, or something close. The house we settled on had a view over a graveyard and was less than an hour's walk from the CBD. Then my wife was turned down from the promotion shed previously been promises, we got cold feet and pulled out of the deal. We looked at our lives and decided to move back to the town we went to uni. Within a few weeks we had bought a house for $95k. We earned the same while living in both cities. in the first market we were going to push ourselves to 100%, while in the second we could manage the mortgage comfortably. We could have spent $350k in the second market too, but why bother? My point is you can't map income to a house. Income serves as a cap, that you simply can't spend over a certain amount, but sensible people spend less than that cap. Someone buying a $90k house might earn $25k and they might earn $120k, or anything in between.

Question: Why aren't all the EV charging stations using the same chargers?
Answer: Annoying isn’t it! Just a few weeks ago I went to use a public charger, only to see that it had the wrong connector for my car. I’m assuming it’ll be fixed in the next few years. My bet is the EU will mandate a particular standard and vehicle manufacturers will grumble but comply.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: How big a solar panel and battery do you need to fully charge an electric car like the plug-in Range Rover?
Answer: My parents ran a similar calculation. They put in solar panels and no battery. That power is used to charge the car, heat the water or whatever else is using electricity, or sell it back to the grid. They calculated how many kWh their car uses in a regular day, as well as the same for hot water per day. They then purchased enough solar panels to produce this on an ordinary cloudy day. From memory it worked out to ten 400W panels for them, but you'd really need to work it out for yourself. How far do you drive the Range Rover on a typical day? Convert that to kWh, not the car's range. One thing that tripped them up and will likely be a problem for you is the Range Rover (and their Mitsubishi) is a hybrid rather than an electric vehicle. The ICE motor can't handle months without use and the fuel in the tank degrades. You have to do a long trip at least every couple months or you'll damage your car.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: Why isn’t profit sharing more common in businesses and corporations? Should it be required?
Answer: My experience is that most employees don't want to be in business, they're there to work hard in exchange for some cash. Sure, they'd love a bonus if the company does well, but they are not happy with having their income docked if the company does badly. Offer an employee $5,000 or a 70% chance of making $10,000 and most will take the safe money. There is nothing inherently wrong with a profit sharing model, but at least in my experience the owner giving up the profit values it much more than the employee getting it. There is a business around the corner from me where the owner retired without finding a buyer willing to pay enough. Rather than drop his price, he ended up gifting the business to his long term staff and effectively creating a co-op. Athat worked and the company is still operating but again, I suspect that if he'd demanded a nominal payout then the employees would simply have got jobs elsewhere instead. Mandating it would certainly be interesting since it would level the playing field. You'll no longer have employees choosing the safer all-cash job since they all include the profit share. Yeah, I can see that working… I don't think it would ever happen organically because I don't think employees value it as much as they should, but it could come in if it was mandated by the government much like minimum wage. You would need to work out how you compensate shareholders when you introduce it since you're effectively forcing them to gift shares to staff, or more precisely probably to unions.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: Why are the rich judged as filthy rich?
Answer: Let’s say you’re really into cars. You save up for many years and buy a McLaren. It’s your pride and joy, you tell everyone about it (often at length) and are frequently saving up to buy track time or cover repairs and maintenance. There’s nothing wrong with this - you’ve got something that’s important to you and you’ve prioritised it in your life. Let’s say your rich friend sees your car, says ‘that’s kinda neat’ and buys one for himself. He then lits it sit at the dealer for months at a time when he’s not using it, and frequently even forgets he has one. He does the same with everything - not only ignoring the price but not really engaging either because that level of opulence is routine. Filthy rich is where you swap from having enough to having more than enough. When money loses meaning it becomes much harder to appreciate the value of hard work.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: Everybody talks about how much they are saving with an electric car. What about the time it take to charge it?
Answer: In the last six months I’ve had to wait for my car to charge twice. The vast majority of the time I plug in when I get home which takes almost no time; the vast majority of the rest of the time I’m on some sort of trip and I coincide recharging the car for when I need a rechard too. Once I stopped for breakfast and plugged my car in to charge. After breakfast something had gone wrong with the charger. That day I had to actually wait for the car to charge before I could continue my trip. I sat in the car watching youtube for half an hour which was fine, but I’d rather have been home with my family. Another time I had enough charge to get to my destination but I wanted to play it safe, so I stopped about an hour out for twenty minutes or so. The best analogy I have is to imagine that your gas car really didn’t like being filled up twice on the same day. If you need to do that then it can only be done at a mechanic rather than a regular gas station. That’s roughly what it’s like with an EV - a minor waste of time once every blue moon.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: Hey, I need a bit of advice. Can I hire a maid to help me finish going through the rest of my moving boxes? I am handicapped and need help moving things around. I will pay, I just don’t know if a maid or someone else?
Answer: What I've found is that the more senior someone is, the less tolerant that person is of doing jobs they consider outside their job description. Maids clean and to some extent tidy up, but I suspect you'll find that lifting heavy boxes or working out where things should belong will not be seen as ok. Back when my kids were much younger we looked at getting help around the home. What we found was nannies are not willing to walk the dogs or do the washing, while cleaners are not willing to entertain kids and were not keen on tidying either. I found this weird. If someone wants to pay my hourly rate for me to make coffee, run errands or clean the office then I'll do it to the best of my ability. You're probably better with a home assistance service, or posting the requirements to a generic job board such as the one for students.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: If an electric car (EV) under warranty catches fire and burns down a building, is the EV manufacturer responsible for the damage to the property?
Answer: There was a real EV fire near me recently, so I can no longer say that I’ve never seen it happen. A woman had, ahem, consumed some restricted substances in large quantities before deciding to drive home in her Tesla. This wasn’t the smartest idea - what she’d consumed had a significant impact on her driving. She had several moderately significant crashes on the way home. That didn’t stop her, it turns out you can bounce off a concrete wall and just keep driving as long as you don’t care about minor details like damage. Anyway, as she was driving over a bridge the car finally decided it had had enough and forced her to come to a stop and get out, and shortly afterwards it burst into flames quite spectacularly. In this case her car probably would be under warranty, but blowing up when you’ve kept driving after a crash is not covered by warranty. I also don’t believe the woman’s insurance will be useful due to the substances she’d consumed beforehand, so I think she’ll be on the hook for all damage. Hypothetically a car with a manufacturing defect which causes it to burn down a house while charging? My guess is that first insurance would kick in, and the insurance company would talk to the car manufacturer… and I’d guess the EV manufacturer would cover it.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: Does charging a Tesla raise your electric bill?
Answer: Intellectually it must. However for my household we literally never noticed. Doing some rough numbers, I drive about 200 miles in an average week (30kWh). I charge on a cheap overnight plan ($0.07/kW). So it costs me roughly $2 per week, or $10/month. If I was paying a more normal amount for electricity then my costs would double. My parents don't pay anything, they put in a really cheap solar system (no batteries) and that's enough to charge theirs.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: Should gas-powered vehicles be banned completely in the future? If yes, is this a violation of people's freedom, especially those who are fond of internal combustion?
Answer: Personally I really dislike bans. As much as electric cars will dominate, there will always be niches they fit poorly. Maybe hydrogen will close those and maybe not. However outright banning? Why bother. It'd be like banning horses after the introduction of the car. I do think the tax on gas is insufficient to pay for the health and environmental problems it causes, and I think that should be increases, but perhaps not yet while it's such a political hot potato.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: What are the main motivations for buying a BYD electric car?
Answer: My aunt bought one. She chose it because it has most of the benefits of a Tesla model Y at a substantial discount. It's a true electric car from an electric car company, not some bastardized transition. It has plenty of space. It's no frills.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: How does EvGo compare with Tesla's superchargers?
Answer: Firstly I’d like to highlight Steve Baker’s excellent answer. There’s three downsides to third party charges that I’ve noticed: This is mostly Tesla’s fault but they are not integrated into the GPS. If you navigate somewhere and need a charge then it won’t go via a third party charger. This is particularly annoying when a third party charger is simply the only option. Related to this, your car won’t precondition the battery when you’re approaching a third-party fast charger. This makes the first five minutes of charging almost useless. Tesla already has my credit card details and it auto-detects my car. Third party chargers require me to launch a special app, choose the charger and click start. Perhaps it only takes a minute but it’s still annoying. The failure rate of third party chargers is (anecdotally) far worse. I’ve had a charger where I’ve rocked up only to see that it’s reporting a fault. I’ve had several that I simply couldn’t get to work and had to notify the company. I’ve had one that was behind scaffolding so it might be fine but nobody could use it. I’ve had several where they just assumed you’d have your own charging cables. I’ve never had an issue with Tesla chargers.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: Was anyone happy after selling their Tesla?
Answer: Sure, I was reading the story about someone yesterday. They had a high paying job which required them to do a lot of driving and they got a Tesla Some months later, the stress of that job proved too much for them and they took a different one which paid $30k/year less. They were far happier in their new job but unfortunately the pay drop was making the $1,700/month car payment unsustainable. Anyway they were happy. No more $1700/month.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: Do Tesla owners own another vehicle for times when they need to take longer trips?
Answer: Generally Tesla owners do own another vehicle because most are coming from two vehicle households and the Tesla is the last car they purchased. It’s more interesting to look at the car they purchase next - will they replace the second car with a second Tesla? That’s certainly the scenario we’re in, having replaced my car with a Tesla while my wife is still driving her older car. I only have a sample-of-one to go off here, my parents purchased a Tesla and later replaced their plugin hybrid with… another plugin hybrid. I was really surprised - I had expected them to get a Tesla Model Y for a bunch of reasons, probably the biggest is that driving a Tesla is different from driving a Mitsubishi, and why have the mental effort of jumping between two different ways of driving. I strongly prefer to take the Tesla on longer trips because the autopilot is awesome on the open road. Note that a Tesla on a long trip is just as expensive as a gas car (at least where I am) because supercharging is really expensive. I’m taking the Tesla because I like the autopilot enough to justify the hassle of planning where to recharge.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: As a software engineer, how do I build up my career so I can start my own company?
Answer: Firstly I'd strongly encourage you to think about exactly what you're trying to achieve. For example I'm a data scientist and after starting my company I get to: clean toilets, shop for office supplies, manage the cloud infrastructure, write HR policies, review contracts, manage accounts receivable, provide financial reporting, sell the team's skills, deal with any concerns or complaints, run payroll… Notably absent from that list is doing data science. You're a software engineer, do you want to spend your time doing the things I listed above or software engineering? Be extremely careful what you ask for, because when most devs say they want to start their own company, my experience is they mean they want to own shares in a startup while still doing software engineering. Also are you sure you want to own the company? My company doesn't do internal software development now, so I'm going back a few years for this story. We had delivered a major project by working like crazy. We had built up a good profit doing so and that money was sitting in the bank. We had a choice: disperse this money, or follow the plan and use it to fund the next phase (turning our service into a SaaS product). We did the latter and hired a bunch of devs. You will already be familiar with the management stuff, but I want to focus on how every week I was running payroll using money that would otherwise have gone to my family. When an employee spent say 30 minutes complaining to another employee that we should be using JS rather than C#. Again, you're a dev so you already know that intervening would be stupid micromanagement. Nobody works welk when their boss forces their nose to the grindstone, but it's really hard to watch and not think: 'I just paid $100 for that rant’. Ultimately the savings were spent and I'd done a lousy job of selling the product. We were nowhere near breakeven. We decided I should move away from the product and leave it to the developers, instead spending my time consultant and using the profit to fund the product development. Every month I'd bust my gut, just to watch all the income go to someone else. Month after month you do this mental calculation: look at how much I chose to invest from my personal funds into the business this month. If I'd never started then look how much money I'd have. Every month my co-founder said we are really close and I should be patient. I'm sure as a dev you've worked for free before, maybe with other people that were also working for free. But I'm betting you've never paid people to work on your project. Devs are expensive. Ultimately I pulled the plug, never knowing if we were 'just three more months from a breakthrough.’ all that money was gone. You say you want to start a company. Again, the company owner is the one on the hook for the financial impact of every decision. Is that what you want? Do you have enough personal savings to provide the company with sufficient runway? This answer is already too long and I haven't explicitly answered how to do this. If the above has not dissuaded you then you're welcome to message me. Briefly though the two main skills you need are general management, and sales. I got my experience running a small business unit. You could work on getting promoted to a similar role in a company that does software engineering. Basically any role with P&L responsibility.

Question: I have been trying to get into a freelancer job in the past 5 months but it seems impossible. Can you put me through?
Answer: It’s circular. If you have a reputation as being successful doing freelance work then you can get more. If you don’t then very few people are willing to take a risk on you - a bad freelancer can cause a lot of damage, even if for example they were working for free. Broadly the free market works and there are about as many freelanders as people wanting that work. It’s hard to break in because there is not a massive amount of unmet demand. As a consultant I’m quite often given jobs that would otherwise go to freelancers and you can bet those companies would have much rather hired an internal at a fraction of the cost. One way to break in is to get a job at a successful contracting company. These have already developed a reputation, and so can sell your time in situations you wouldn’t be able to sell it yourself. Pay attention and after a few years there you should have both the skills and reputation to do it without their help. Also pay attention to your contract, most will not allow you to get a freelance role at a company they’ve contracted you to, but for example if your main contact at that company moves to another company then they might be keen to hire you over there too.

Question: Are college professors paid handsomely?
Answer: I tried to get into academia after graduating. At the time I was living in a university town, and the pay for an associate lecturer was plenty for a comfortable life. I was unable to get a permanent role and the pay for the various fixed term contracts I got was substantially lower, but enough to live a modest life. I moved to a city for work and my house here costs literally five times what we paid back in the university town. It's also impossible to sustain getting to work every day without a car whereas previously we walked, and everything else is just more expensive too. Academics here are paid exactly the same as they were back in my quiet little university town. That is, a junior academic is not paid enough to live independently. Two living together would be ok, or someone that has been promoted to a senior level. A senior lecturer would just have enough income to afford to buy a modest two bedroom unit near the university over about 25–30 years. To be fair, the work is awesome. Preparing for and giving lectures to adults that are mostly interested and keen to be there. You'd have to pay me to not do research, and even applying for grants isn't that bad apart from the stress. It's understandable that more interesting jobs pay less.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: How do I discipline myself when it comes to saving?
Answer: The way I do it is by not using the word saving. I spend every dollar I earn. Just… some dollars get spent a little later than others. For example this month I spent $500 on buying a new car, and $618 on replacing the house roof. Think of it as like having a payment plan for absolutely everything. The reason this works is that it makes it impossible to take money out of savings. Every single purchase has to come from somewhere in the budget. Yesterday my wife spent $100 on some books for my daughter to continue encouraging her reading; that wasn’t money we had budgeted, and so I had to pick a category such as our upcoming trip and suck $100 out of it. The one (arguable) exception is retirement. I treat every $1,000 saved as buying a $4/month. Every month I compare my monthly budget to the amount of retirement income I have saved, and am slowly working on getting them closer. Again though, it’s not some vague nebulus savings, but a concrete target with a clear chart of progress.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: Is studying computer science in college worthwhile with AI like ChatGPT replacing programming jobs and evolving rapidly each year? Should I explore other fields to avoid job market struggles and potential difficulty in job retention after graduation?
Answer: We had a similar discussion at home currently. I did CS when I went through, and my son is choosing which course to enrol in now. One of the things we talked about was whether a slightly different degree would be more or less impacted by upcoming improvements in AI. Ultimately he decided to do the same course he was planning to do before the discussion. Every field is going to have substantial upheaval over the next few years - I was reading a post on Quora from eight years ago on what fields would be affected last by AI, and every one of them was currently being substantially impacted. My point is that we cannot predict what the future holds even looking forward eight years, let alone for an entire working career. One advantage of studying CS is you’ll have a better understanding of how AI works, and therefore will be in a better position to adjust what you do as AI advances. A CS major comes out of university with a good understanding of algorithms, while a biology major will come out of university with a good understanding of biology. AI will change both biology and software engineering, but at least the CS major will see more how the AI is integrating, and be able to shift focus to where it is weaker. RIght now (May 2023) tools like ChatGPT suck at software development because they don’t ask for clarification when they’re unclear, and so you get code which doesn’t work. It’s called ChatGPT, there’s nothing stopping it saying ‘Hang on a sec, I’ve got no idea what to do in this edge case, how would you expect me to handle that?’. Stochastic parrots and all that… it currently outputs even when it’s lost, but this is a fixable deficiency. Once this happens I expect it to be an enormously valuable programming assistant. Software development is going to change massively in the years after you graduate. That might be a reason to stay away from CS if it were the only field going through this, but it’s going to impact every single field. I’m not confident that I can correctly predict which fields will be more or less impacted, and therefore where you’d be better off if you’re looking for a safe career. Two possible suggestions would be to consider the trades, which I personally think will be the last/least affected, and to really focus on learning how to learn rather than what the market demands now. If you’re adaptable then you’ll be in a much better position to get through this. A proper university education should give you this. I mentioned the trades briefly above. Robotics and AI are entering the trades now, and people with the skills to work better with them will do better in the future than people who ignore them and treat AI as a white-collar disruptor. The same thinking applies to every field - get a job as a teacher and your role will increasingly be about whatever aspect AI doesn’t do well. Currently that’s motivating and re-engaging students.

Question: Gwyneth Paltrow's website, Goop, is selling $90 prenatal vitamins. Doctors say they are the same ones from the drugstore. Do you think her website's aim is to be aspirational, like she claims, or do you think she is a charlatan?
Answer: Your question makes it sound like aspirational is the opposite of being a charlatan. Everyone selling vitamins is a charlatan. You just poop them out again. There is a reason they aren't called medicine and managed by the FDA, and that's because they are very safe — much like sugar pills. There are situations where vitamins are good for you, but the vast majority of people having them would do just as well with a placebo. These vitamins are clearly aspirational. Gwyneth Paltrow's fans aspire to be connected closer to her. These vitamins are expensive because they are branded. Most of what you are paying for the brand. I was at the dealership of my old car some years ago and saw a device for sale to find your car keys. I'd recently bought a chipolo for this exact purpose and like to buy genuine things. After a bit of digging I found I was being sold a regular chipolo in the shape of the car's insignia, for four times the price of a regular chipolo. It's exactly the same thing, you are paying for the brand.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: Who are these globe trotting digital nomads? Do certain nations in the world accommodate them with visas, so they can live there & work on the laptop? Are Canada & Australia far stricter & would not introduce that type of visa, & do they contribute?
Answer: I have employed two and am going to assume they are representative for this answer. Firstly they are both young, highly educated and with skills that are in very high demand. They are exactly the kind of people that every nation is trying to attract, some other country has done the hard work educating them and now they have a long productive career ahead, so they can get a visa essentially anywhere. Secondly, they are often working for companies in different countries to where they are living. This means that, from the perspective of the country they are living, they are essentially on holiday. The criteria for a six month holiday visa is much less strict than for a 'working’ visa. Tourists are walking ATMs.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: I've heard that car dealers don't make much money selling new vehicles. Somehow, I find that hard to believe. Are they not making money? And if not, why stay in the business?
Answer: Let's say you sell a shiny new Mercedes for $80,000. You had to buy that car from Daimler, how much would you guess they sell it to you for? Further, you have to pay a substantial lease in the land and building, and every month you don't sell a car it's value goes down which you'll have to wear. Pay for car sales is normally commission on profit, so I'll ignore it here. It's easy to think of the $80k, but take away those costs and there will not be much left, or even a loss. The profit comes because customers rarely pay just the sticker price. Whether it's finance, add-ons or service, you have an almost captive customer and so the margins are very high. It's very similar to the razor blade business model. Note that Tesla does not use dealers, and EVs in general need less service, so the whole business model is being upended. Its not clear yet where we will end up.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: Are Tesla vehicles suited for the rental market? Is there a learning curve or could a customer just hop in and drive off?
Answer: I personally think a five minute tour of the car is pretty much essential if it’s someone’s first time. Here’s how you put it in drive; push twice for cruise control. Here’s the voice assistant - you can use that whenever you forget where something is such as opening the glove box. Also taking your foot off the accelerator is like pressing the break, you need your foot on a little if you want to cruise. I remember my wife commenting when I first got my car that I was a bit jerky, and a few weeks later that I’d improved significantly. That’s more comfort than safety, although the speed at which it takes off takes some getting used to. Without a tour I’d expect someone to manage to drive away but I think there’d be significant safety risks.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: Does Tesla have an edge in the EV world anymore? Considering they don't have longest battery range, nor best autonomous driving, nor fastest accelerating car?
Answer: Range is not why people choose a particular car, at least beyond the very bottom end of the market. The ‘fastest acceleration’ is a marketing game, and again irrelevant to most people buying a car. Tesla continue to have the best autonomous driving, but like your previous two points, most customers don’t really care. The real reasons people buy one brand over another are confusing and contradictory. A lot comes down to price of course, and beyond that there’s a nebulous concept of how closely you match the brand. Do you feel like a Tesla person, or like a Rivian person? If you’ve always bought Ford then the F150-lightning will naturally appeal. People that identify with wanting value-for-money will like the Kia EV6. Does Tesla embarrass you with Elon’s eccentricities, while BYD’s ‘cheap and functional’ is right up your alley? Think about the difference between the Volvo XC40 EV and the Polestar. One is classic Volvo - solid, safe and reliable, while the other is designed for “the desire to explore how racing technology could be applied to the performance of Volvo street cars”. What’s Tesla’s brand identity? Minimalist; Sexy; Edgy; Technology led; Disrupting. I think Tesla’s attempt to remove parking sensors is particularly telling: “Include only what’s necessary, even if everyone else has it and our customers demand it”. Let’s go back to your ‘fastest acceleration’ comment - nobody actually uses this, but it still sells cars. People like to be associated with crazy fast cars. It’s all weird psychology stuff. From a technical perspective the hardest part for other manufacturers to copy is the autonomous driving. I know a lot of people talk about the billions of hours of footage Tesla has and how no other manufacturer is close, but time makes everything easier in tech, such as the three billion dollar human genome project in 2003 becoming a $200 test in 2023. I think this will hold out as a unique selling point for Tesla over the next few years, but it will be impossible to sustain in the long term.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: Are there any disadvantages in using robots?
Answer: I know a number of dairy farmers that decided to go robotic rather than hire a contract milker. Their reasoning was more about privacy than money. Robots are expensive. Even amortized over a number of years, they cost about as much as a salary. Having a contract milker means having someone else wandering around your farm every day. Someone that does things their way. Employees always cause headaches. Robotic milking reduces the workload to the point an older farmer can keep going for a few years rather than being forced into selling and retirement. They're still a lot of work. One person I was talking to described it as trading 5am starts for a couple hours fixing machines. They require constant maintenance, you're effectively becoming a mechanic.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: What’s having a Tesla like?
Answer: After the first couple weeks where it is novel… it's a car. You use it to go places, just like whatever car you had before. Never stopping to refuel is nice. Numerous times in the past I was running late for something and ended up ten minutes later. Trips away require slightly more planning, such as checking the place I'm staying has a charger, or finding a supercharger near a nice breakfast place. I like the minimalist interior. I wish it had a HUD (I've ordered a third party one but it's not here yet). I wish there was a button to open the frunk. I think the flat door handles are a gimmick with no benefit. The interior is spacious. I'm still kicking myself for adding a roof rack rather than a tow bar. The cruise control is probably the best part. Driving is substantially less mental energy. OTA updates constantly make the car a little better. Being able to remotely see around the car and getting video footage of any near miss is awesome. The car stopping for every red light or disabled traffic light is really annoying but not quite annoying enough that I've disabled stopping for red. The hill assist and park assist is noticably better than other cars. Summon has the potential to be great but in practice rarely delivers. I love not having services any more. With my old car I felt like I was gambling; sometimes the service would say nothing is wrong and other times they would say that'll be $2,000. Overall I'd say: 75% — it's a car. 10% — EVs are far more convenient than ICE 5% — the exclusively EV manufacturers are better than the old guard 10% — Tesla specifically is good. That's why I have trouble getting excited about a debate on Tesla vs Rivian or similar, at most you're debating the last ten percent.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: What do I do if I don't want to graduate college? I’m scared I will miss meeting new people, being surrounded by people my age, partying, everything. I really think this is the best time of my life and I’m actually terrified to graduate in spring.
Answer: Heh, yeah, I get that. You’re right. You will meet people in a workplace but it’s much harder. There’s much more variation in people so you’ll find far fewer are your sort, Additionally many already have their circle of friends and are simply not at a stage of their life where they’re looking at expanding it. More important, people have far less time. You’ll struggle to spend time with them because you’ll be busy with work, and they’ll struggle for the same reason. People tend to commute for longer to work than they did for college, and there’s a lot more housework too. Plus looking after kids is a massive time sink. You’ll make it happen because the alternative is being lonely. But yeah, I agree, it probably is the best time of your life. You can always do what I did and try and become a permanent graduate student, and/or join the staff. One thing I found doing that though is that I’d make awesome friends and then a year or two later they’d bugger off into the workforce and changing cities.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: What Personal Computer (PC) software you were familiar with before Microsoft got into the business?
Answer: I was just a kid when Microsoft started. Their MS-DOS quickly took over, to the point that I’m having to think of my earliest memories for experiences on a computer that predate them. Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: Why does a man think of earning money even though he has unlimited money?
Answer: My friend has had enough money to retire ever since I met him. His net worth at the time was around $10m, so invested modestly he could generate an annual income of $400k. He’s one of the hardest workers I know and is a little obsessed about money, always chasing more. Unlike me he has ambitions to increase his net worth significantly and is tackling projects that could double his wealth or bankrupt him. This makes very little sense to me; my focus is always around having enough, and there is virtually no benefit in having more than enough. I really struggle with the idea of risking enough in the pursuit of more. I think there’s two things going on: He went through a most of his adult years trying to grow a business that gradually became worth a lot on paper but wasn’t paying him. His whole adult life until shortly before I met him had required him to actively seek out ways to make money, so he had literal decades of developing this habit. His attitude towards accumulating money is very different to mine. He treats it as part of the game of life and the pursuit of happiness, so if he’s accumulating money then he’s doing well with that facet of his life. Mine is that money buys stability, and once you have that then deeper foundations are pointless - your focus has to shift. Anyway this is obviously sample-of-one stuff and I don’t know how representative he is. I find it useful to remember because it highlights that my attitude towards money is not the only valid option. When I look around at the big projects that happen, I realise both that it’s good many of them happen, and that there is absolutely no circumstance that I would have started that project so the world clearly needs people with different attitudes.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: I'm looking for a sponsor. When I finish my travel, I will pay back his money. What can I do?
Answer: Some years ago I used to invest in P2P loans. The local government has since made them illegal but this story is why I personally stopped. The platform I was using provided the stuff you'd expect such as credit risk and the interest rate I'd get, and also why the person wants the money. I'll try and reproduce the quote from memory: Hey, I'd like the money to shout my mom a holiday back home. My mom and I don't have much money and she's worked really hard for two years to pay for my apprenticeship. Now I've graduated I want to give her the money back with this surprise gift. Sweet right? The guy who posted this was obvious not that into arithmetic but I am. Because of his low wage he was given a low monthly payment and long term. Add in the application fee and high risk insurance policy and he was borrowing almost $2k at 35% interest over three years. His payments were going to cripple him financially for three years, plus thanks to interest he is paying for the trip almost three times. She busted her gut for two years to get him an apprenticeship and he's going to do the same to get her a $1200 holiday and make me some money. By the time I read his story, the algorithm had already arranged for me to lend him the money, I was reading it after the fact. I couldn't cope with the idea I was screwing over people's future and left but of course someone would have taken my place. Coming back to you, my advice is simple: don't do it. Don't borrow money. Save up and pay for your own holiday. Borrowing divorces the hard work from the benefit, making it really easy to overspend because you can't judge the cost. The guy in my story got one holiday and paid for three. I bet his mom would have preferred a holiday a year for three years. There are a handful of situations in life where you need something now enough to justify paying extra. You can hardly come a few months late to a funeral when you don't have the savings. For everything else, there's patience.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: What makes you financially free?
Answer: I have low expenses. Or more accurately I have average expenses on a high income. I have no desire to spend money on luxuries. My main hobbies are playing go and frisbee, both of which are essentially free. I own my house and car. I live in a country with decent universal healthcare. I read a post criticising the FIRE movement as basically living like a pauper: Is The F.I.R.E Movement A Scam? Ignoring the inflationary headline, I find that all those expensive things are fun when you first try them, but they don’t ‘spark any more joy’ after the initial novelty. Make being frugal a hobby, and living efficiently becomes fun rather than a chore. I think part of it is that I really enjoy my work. A lot of people hate their job and use fancy purchases as a mix of reward and distraction. I read a post I wrote on Quora five years ago where I was stressed out by the huge debt/risk that I’d taken on buying a large (to me) business. At the time I knew I would need to maintain my high income for five to ten years for the debt to be repaid. I’m not there yet, but I’m close enough to see the light at the end of the tunnel. I certainly have problems in my life but none of them can be helped by spending money.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: Does everyone who has a PhD degree (in any subject) have above average intelligence?
Answer: I saw a study that the mean IQ score of PhD graduates was two standard deviations above average. Assuming this is correct and nothing else is going on, that means about 97.5% of PhD graduates will have average or higher intelligence. 2.5% isn't a lot, but it's also far from zero.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: How can I get my employer an annual salary adjustment in the employment contract to compensate for inflation, increasing professional experience, and avoid salary negotiations? What number should I use, and how can I convince the employer?
Answer: A good employer will do this. They know that underpaying employees leads to resentment and quitting so they proactively monitor and update. A bad employer pays as little as they can get away with, only giving raises when their hand is forced. Realistically almost all employers are somewhere in the middle, missing when you achieve performance improvements and not noticing changes in the market. Given how much difference salary makes to the employee, it is in your interest to keep your employer on track, gentle pointing out if they fall behind. Many recruiters will provide this information to you freely since they know that if the employee fails to act then you'll go to them looking for another job. That's the other part of what you should do. If your employer doesn't step up with a little prodding then find a better one.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: If I always invest 10% of my salary from age 18, is there a calculator for how much I'll have aged 55?
Answer: There are many calculators. To be accurate the calculator has to take into account the variation in your income and in investment returns. What you're looking for is not so much an estimate but a probabilistic distribution of possible returns.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: Are fruit pickers qualified to apply for residency after 6 months of working in New Zealand?
Answer: No. Check out the casual agricultural worker visa and working holiday visa. Neither has a path to residency. You have to apply for a different (points-based) visa if you want to stay longer.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: I’ve been offered a position that pays $40k more. I love my current position and the company, but I do more work with less pay. I am afraid of leaving and not being happy just because the company pays more. How should I approach this?
Answer: You've been offered a position. That means you searched for suitable jobs, brushed off your resume, applied, went through the interviews, and negotiated a salary. The time to check the new company's culture was during the interview: “have you got any questions for us?” was your opening. If you love your position and company then don't apply elsewhere. There are numerous ways to baseline your salary and now if you don't accept the new job then you will burn bridges. The recruiter will remember how you wasted their time. Also, unless your salary is in the hundreds of thousands, a $40k difference is huge. You wouldn't get that through a market rate review. Take the new job and learn two lessons. Firstly if you want a raise then make a case at your current company, and secondly if you are worried if another job is good, then check during the interview process.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: Do people have to pay to have electric cars charged?
Answer: Where I live, the cost of electricity between 11pm and 6am is so low that it's effectively free. Power plants can optimise their output for peak times but they can't be shut down entirely, so much of this overnight power is wasted Those seven hours of extremely cheap electricity are enough to charge my car 70 miles. So provided I didn't drive more than 70 in the previous day I can refill essentially for free. If course there is no such thing as free electricity. It's currently a waste product because supply exceeds demand but that will change as EV adoption grows. I've also been toying with buying batteries for the house that I charge overnight but haven't because I expect the bargain price to be gone in a few years.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: What attitude do atheists have toward a hesitant atheist? He sometimes believes and doesn't.
Answer: Atheists do not believe in gods. That it. It’s not some special club where they’re trying to get more people to join. If someone wants to be ‘half-atheist’ (aka agnoistic), then I don’t see why that would bother an atheist because such a person is not going to go around proselytising. The normal atheist attitude is that a person’s beliefs are their own personal thing, and they don’t cause any harm as long as the person keeps it to themselves and out of sight.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: My boyfriend has been financially unstable for years. I have ran out of savings and gotten into credit card debt trying to help him. I love him and want to be supportive but the situation isn’t getting any better. What can I do?
Answer: Being supportive does not mean giving him money. Supportive means being there to give him a hug when he screws up. Think of a parent on the sideline cheering on their kid - they don’t run out into the field and help directly or criticise the kid for making mistakes. It means being the one that says “I know you’re trying so hard“. Your boyfriend will make mistakes and run out of money again. It’s up to you to say ‘I’m sorry but I won’t contribute to your share. I’m here to support you doing this, not to do it for you’. You’ll need to make sure that your finances are separate, that your name is not listed as guarantor on any of this stuff such as the lease. You will need to work out what your share is. For example if you’re in a high paying job then the two of you might decide your share might be all of the food, utilities and lease. His share is then limited to things like his phone, clothing and other incidentals. For example if you can’t afford the rent without his contribution then you’ll need to move, because it’s clear that you can’t rely on him financially. A lot of people break up over finances - it’s a big pain being the stable rock for someone else, and it’s over to you to decide if the relationship is worth it. You’re basically parenting him, and people want an equal partner in a relationship rather than a child. My assumption is that he’s a decent adult in other areas of his life to justify this.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: Is a reverse mortgage a good idea if you have to cease working?
Answer: I love the idea of reverse mortgages in theory, but in practice the lousy rates offered by all major players make me hesitant about ever recommending them. If you own your own home then you can live in it, rent free, for as long as you like. Then when you die the house is included in your assets and can be sold. You don’t need the money from the house sale when you’re dead, you need it when you’re still alive… and reverse mortgages are a way to tap into that equity. The trouble is that people often live a really long time, and reverse mortgages have a provision guaranteeing you can stay in your house rent free. Put those together and the only way to make the numbers work is to charge you a high rate of interest on the reverse mortgage. Essentially you continue to live there rent free, but rather than selling your house for say $500k when you die, you instead get $200k upfront.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: Should people in big cities use the EVs and people in the more rural areas drive the ICE vehicles?
Answer: That was how it worked about ten years ago when the first EVs came out, back when they were only suitable up to a range of maybe 50 miles or so. Plenty of rural people travel further than that daily, but almost none travel more than 250 miles most days. Nowadays the only two large group of people better buying a new ICE car are those with no home charging, and those that routinely tow a long distance. My guess is the first group will shrink as chargers are put into more apartment garages, while the second group will remain poorly served by EVs.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: When will electric vehicles be automatically rechargeable?
Answer: Ah yes, the robotic pump, as seen at gas stations across the world. These exist you know, the tech to recharge a car (gas or electric) is the same and it’s been around for years. Give me $20k and I’ll even arrange an installer for you. What’s missing is consumer demand. Would you pay $20k to have your car recharge itself? Would you even pay $2k? Think about what’s needed - A number of servos to hold and move things tidily, and some simple vision to spot where to go. “The cost of a robotic arm varies depending on the type of arm, its capabilities, and the accessories and peripherals needed to operate it. Simple single-axis robots can cost as little as $3,000, while more advanced articulated robots …”. Charging a EV would require movement on two axes, which would put it at around $10k, but it would also benefit from massive economies of scale which I’d guess would make a 10x difference and bring the final price down to $1k eventually. Every technology goes through a phase where early adopters pay a premium, and then everyone else gets it for cheaper. Right now the early adopters are staying away because it’s too expensive. Right now, autonomous charging would save typical owners maybe ten seconds a day and very few people are rich or geeky enough to make that trade. My guess is this will change when parked vehicle summoning becomes much better. Imagine your car coming out from the parking garage and picking you up. Once the tech to achieve this is available, who would want to go into a parking garage ever again? Get dropped off at the entrance and the car sorts out parking. At that point charging goes from being a ten second task to a major inconvenience and my bet is these garages will be the early adopters. I’d give it five years.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: Are Canada & Australia mainly uninhabitable, or could they build it up & develop it more like the USA throughout if they wanted to?
Answer: You mean… could they develop it more like the flyover states? It’s possible to build a city in a desert. Check out Vegas for example. It’s hard, and it is expensive, and it requires a constant inflow of new money to sustain it. So yeah, Australia could do that… and to some extent it does with Camberra. Could it happen in Canada? The capital of Northwest Territories is Yellowknife with a population of just 20k. The climate looks brutal, getting a little too warm in summer and incredibly code in winter. It would grow if you put money in, it’s far more a case of people not wanting to invest the money. Development like America would really require farming. The thing that keeps all those small towns going is that they’re supporting a local (farming) community. I’m not sure what you’d grow that only thrives in deserts or extremes of temperatures, but work that out and you should see growth.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: Why is Auckland so populated compared to the rest of New Zealand?
Answer: Mostly I think it’s circular. Want a job in a city with more than half a million people in it? You have one choice. From a company’s perspective, want to be where the vast majority of skilled labour is and again you just have one choice. Get born to someone that moved to Auckland for work and you’ll have family in Auckland. Moving away will be that much harder because you’ll also be losing easy access to family. There was a serious attempt to counter this way back in the 70s, with the government deliberately funding infrastructure projects outside Auckland. That was a long time ago. Also the weather is nicer in Auckland than a lot of the country.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: Why are we considering AI as a threat?
Answer: Improvements in AI will change things. Change might be good overall but there will be people caught in the middle. Say I use AI to make a call centre more efficient, and the bank decides to retain all staff and simply spend longer with customers / reduce wait times… that’ll lead to more customers staying and that in turn will lead to staff being made redundant at other banks. We all live and work in a word with minimal use of AI. We’re all joining a world with much higher use. Things are going to change, and that’s scary.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: Why are some people going back to petrol cars?
Answer: Name anything and you’ll find people doing it. The more I study data, the more I realise that nothing applies to everyone. People with EVs were surveyed a few years ago to ask if their next car would be an EV. The answer was overwhelmingly yes - even more people are sticking with EVs than iPhone users stick with iPhone. Digging into those that are planning to change, the most common reason is they thought using a public charger would be fine but they have found the reality to be a hassle. EVs are quiet, reliable, fast to accelerate, etc. but it’s very rare nowadays to hear someone say complain their car is too loud, breaks down too much, too slow to start, etc. i.e. there are many things that EVs do better than petrol cars which people don’t actually care much about. What people do care about is never visiting a petrol station again, and paying far less for fuel. Take those away and EVs lose much of their shine.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: Why is math so hard and boring for me?
Answer: Why is math so hard? Perhaps you’re working at the wrong level? We tend to push people at a fixed rate, and if you fall behind then it’s almost inevitable that you will continue to fall further behind. Another possibility is your boredom is making it hard for you to concentrate. boring? The two most likely candidates are bad teaching - nobody likes rote learning, and that your personality is to enjoy things only where you can see the immediate application. Do you enjoy brain teasers? If so then your issue with maths is likely to be bad teaching. If not then maybe you are more suited to practical things where abstract thought is unnecessary.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: Why do people want to emigrate to Australia? It's mainly desert.
Answer: Er… yeah, sure. It’s mostly desert. So what? Virtually nobody goes into the desert. You could double the size of that desert, or shrink it by half, and it wouldn’t affect interest in immigration. Australia might be mostly desert, but everyone that goes there is focused on the little bits that are not desert. This same logic applies to most countries in the world - take Canada for example, it’s mostly wilderness. You could double or halve the size of that wilderness and it would barely affect Canadian immigration. What matters is what you see, not the great big empty area few people pay attention to.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: Why do so many kiwis choose to live in Australia? New Zealand is such a beautiful country
Answer: Money. Pick a profession that both countries are short of - say nurses. The starting rate for an enrolled nurse in Australia is, on average, $62,789 (all Australian figures have been converted to $NZ) - nearly $9000 more than in New Zealand. They max out at around $73,930 - almost $17,000 more than in New Zealand. Registered nurses and midwives in Australia start out on average at $71,260 - already more than many with a few years' experience here get - and max out at around $100,000. Most states don't offer quite that much, but the average is skewed by massive pay packets for nurses in ACT ($131,670) and the Northern Territory ($145,300). When I decided it was time to leave Wellington, my wife and I looked seriously at whether we’d be better in Auckland or Australia. Airfares were cheap at the time so visiting family was similar in cost, and the pay in Sydney was substantially higher. We ultimately chose Auckland, but I remember wondering if we’d really screwed up when we first arrived and the best place we could to live find was crappy rental at $800/wk. I was earning double the median wage ($120k) but my wife wasn’t working as she was at home with our youngest, so our household income was pretty typical. After tax, superannuation (Kiwisaver) and student loan repayments I was taking home $72K and paying 55% in rent, to leave $32k for everything else. That compares to Australia where we’d have had over $50k of disposable income. We were ok and being in NZ was important to us but run the same formula on a $100k income and you’re left with $22k spending money per year, compared to $40k in Australia. At that point you’re seriously tight, and well, Australia starts to look pretty good.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: What do you think about people using food stamps to buy fresh seafood?
Answer: There’s two ways to answer this: pragmatic and moral. From a pragmatic perspective, every attempt to artificially affect the market always backfires. Food stamps that can’t buy certain groceries will push up the cost of what they can buy and down the cost of what they can’t. Further the admin required to enforce that is nightmarish, can you imagine the software system which goes ‘ah nope, transaction contains seafood, so we must reject that payment’. What you’ll end up with is the large supermarkets supporting it and the smaller grocers saying ‘that’s too hard’, so effectively the person is banned from the smaller, cheaper grocers. The closest I’ve come to experiencing this firsthand was when I was an undergrad at uni. The government decided students might take their student loan and I don’t know… spend it on hookers or something, so they stopped giving out money and instead only allowed you to buy from the university bookstore. As a consequence I had to spend $1k on textbooks rather than maybe $200 buying second-hand. Morally, how does limiting what can be bought make the world a better place? I guess you’re worrying the person will buy expensive seafood and then not have enough money to eat, requiring a second handout? If someone is eligible for support then how about trusting that they work out what’s best for them. Maybe a little treat of seafood is how they maintain sanity in their life? I find the pragmatic argument is more effective when talking with conservatives. They seem to ‘get’ that the government bureaucracy will screw up any guard rails and that the free market will be more efficient, whereas I find arguing that gifts should be unconditional to be ineffective.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: Is Australia has both skill shortages & jobs that the locals don’t wish to do such as fruit picking, why don’t they just let me in to do that? Always happy to start out on an orchard or in a vineyard to get a foot in the door. A warm & relaxing job.
Answer: You’ll find specialist immigration visas that allow you to get a job helping with harvests and nothing else (Australian Agriculture Visa). You can work on the vineyard, and yeah it is very hot work, and then you’ll be sent home. It’s not a bad choice - the pay is reasonable. It’s not a foot in the door though. Often the people who go are younger and fitter, and they send the money back to their family. In terms of why this isn’t a foot in the door, it all comes back to the visa. Immigration run different tiers of visas with the lowest being for specific events such as fruit picking, followed by unrestricted but time-limited visas, followed by visas that track you through to citizenship. The criteria for one are very different to the criteria for others, and so if you’re not eligible for the ‘critical skills shortage’ visa then getting the agriculture one isn’t going to help much. You could maybe do an amazing job helping out on the farm and get them to sponsor you for a better visa. That route feels hard but at least theoretically possible. Part the problem is you’ll need the farm to sponsor you and if you’re flat out working on the harvest then you will have very little contact with the farm owner.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: My new job offered me $14 and even said that was how much I would make in text message. I check my paychecks 2 months later and it is revealed I make $13.85. What should I do?
Answer: Talk to HR. My guess is it’s a technical deduction and the company truly is paying you $14. It’s just not worth a company lying over 1% - the bad impact it has on employees has far more effect than the 1% costs them.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: Is it possible for a 35 year old man to land himself a 19 or 23 year old lady or would he be far too old for such ladies?
Answer: When I was 22 I had a friend of mine (also 22) move in with an (almost) 40 year old man. So yeah, it happens. Personally I thought it was really creepy. I mean, he was nice enough, but to my 22 year old he seems old, with the male pattern baldness really not helping. But also having a proper professional job and a house and stuff. It was weird. Talking to her she said his age didn’t bother her - he was just him, and he’d falling for her because she was heaps of fun to be around rather than because she was almost half his age. Anyway my point is anyone with any sort of pattern of dating younger women would be waving a massive red flag. See if you’re 21 and he’s 35 then you might be right in his sweet spot now, but in five years you’ll be 26 and you just won’t look or act like 21 any more. Starting a relationship with someone that dates much younger women feels like starting a relationship that comes with a built in time bomb. Why go through that risk.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: My wife is a young dentist. But I don't want her to treat men. Only children and women. I just feel uncomfortable about her treating men. Is it ok?
Answer: My wife is also a dentist. I’m going to ignore the controlling nature of your question and focus on the business side. Could a business that only treated women and children succeed. Yeah, I think it could work in a large enough city. One of the things my wife mentioned is she has some muslim patients who love being able to take off all of the extra headwear since there are no men in the building. Advertise the practice as ‘strictly no men’ and you’ll get women who want a break from guys, as well as women who have weird controlling partners. As much as your question strikes me as weird, I can imagine random weird guys asking similar ones: “My wife is beautiful. I don’t like the idea of her ever being in a room with a man unless I’m there, so how can she go to the dentist?” There are a few ‘women only’ businesses around. I was looking at a taxi service the other day in response to someone whose Uber driver kept hitting on her. It’s an odd niche and excluding half the population is always going to be dubious from a business perspective, but the key for business is to be the best provider of the service for enough customers rather than appealing to everyone. One complication your wife would have is that most good patients come from referrals. With only seeing women you’ve not just eliminated half the potential customers but more important, you’ve effectively eliminated half the potential referrals. This means the practice will have half the growth rate. Note, I’m assuming she is setting up a brand new practice which she’ll own. I can’t imagine any employer tolerating this, or any existing practice surviving the change.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: Would you rather have $2 million in 1850 or $750K today?
Answer: One of the things I’ve discovered about myself is that I prefer being in a similar position to the people around me. Two million dollars in 1850 is an almost incomprehendible amount of money, enough to live life like a king with a large team of servants. Yet I wouldn’t have a washing machine, fridge, car, phone, computer or any of dozens of modern conveniences. Daily life wouldn’t be so bad with servants looking after your clothes, preparing your meals and your bath… but those things are pretty easy with a washing machine, induction hob, and shower. Have I mentioned healthcare yet? The big thing that puts me off though is that I’d be surrounded by people with far less than me. I’d have to assume that every overture of friendship was someone wanting to get at my wealth, and that I’d be one big screw-up away from a life in the gutter. I like being normal. I live in a country with universal healthcare, a (mostly) decent minimum wage, and loads of free activities such as sports grounds and nature walks. Less than a million dollars today is enough to provide a $30k or so ‘income top-up’. Not quite enough to live off unless you’re really frugal, but enough to turn a regular job into a comfortable life. More important is that I’d be hardly worse off if I somehow lost the money. Also the $750k would barely be visible between me and people I interacted with. It seems an easy choice.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: Would you rather have 100,000 in stocks, 100,000 in Gold, or 100,000 in Bitcoin?
Answer: Without any requirement to hold the asset, I’d go for the crypto. Selling stocks that you’ve been gifted isn’t too bad, but you need to prove ownership and it’s a bit of a pain. Selling gold is a big pain, at best the gold is in an exchange and you’re essentially selling stocks. At worst you have to physically take the gold somewhere to be valued. Selling crypto is easy, you just enter the private key and provide your bank account details. This was the original purpose of Bitcoin - it can be transferred from person to person very easily.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: Are you willing to sacrifice your civil liberties for universal healthcare?
Answer: I find it fascinating how when people want to criticize something they make these vague, overgeneralized assertions. Are you willing to sacrifice your liberties for… Which liberty? The right to bear arms? To silence? To the pursuit of happiness? Under universal healthcare I don't have the right to walk into a public hospital and demand medical tests and treatment. Those choices can only be made by my doctor. I'd have to walk into a private hospital to demand that. So really I haven't lost any rights at all. If I want to bankrupt myself then I have the right to much the same medical system as America. I also have the right to another one, where in exchange for slightly less control, I get free healthcare. My bet is that if a free healthcare system opened in America, paid for by tax, then most Americans would happily use their service. I suppose I don't have the right to opt out of paying tax. But again that right is not available to Americans. If they think the government wastes money on pork barrel politics and pointless military then I can't simply refuse to pay.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: Did you hear about Elon Musk's statement on Bill Mahar's show on April 29th that AI, that is, intelligent computers will show people how to live long lives without death?
Answer: No, I didn't hear this. My opinion is that Elon Musk is brilliant at many things, but at others he's a complete and utter idiot. That's probably normal, but what is unusual is Elon can't seem to stop talking on subjects he just isn't very knowledgeable. It's a little like a successful Quoran posting about absolutely everything. It very quickly becomes annoying noise. My response has been to tune him out. I rely on other people to teme if he says something relevant, and that way I don't have to listen to the irrelevant bits. If you do want to know about the future of AI, I'm not sure who to recommend. Honestly, there are an awful lot if people speculating, but I can't think of any that have a particularly good track record.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: How do I ask what happened? I am flying to Australia to meet the man I have been dating for 2.5 years. A month after I bought my ticket, he ghosted me. So now I have a 5-week trip for nothing.
Answer: Hey, on the plus side, Australia is a nice country to visit My personal favourite is Melbourne, but anywhere is fine in winter. It’s just I find some places unbearably hot in midsummer. Go. Enjoy yourself. Forget about this guy who probably isn’t even Australian in the first place. Maybe you’ll meet someone while you’re there, and even if not there’s still helps of fun stuff to do.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: Have Teslas saved more carbon than SpaceX's rocket launches have added back to the atmosphere? Or has SpaceX's activities cancelled out any potential carbon savings from Tesla automobiles? Any back-of-the-envelope calculations anyone? Mr. Musk?
Answer: I am not going to do a back of the envelope calculation, though if you really want one I see others have. The point of SpaceX is that if humanity stays stuck on earth then we will die out. Although some things are better than others, nothing we do is sustainable. This sort of thing happens in life and business too. You get stuck in a rut slowly using your dwindling resources. Musk has made major contributions to help: Making EVs popular to reduce our burn rate; revolutionizing PT through tunnels and autopilot; improving battery tech to increase efficiency; making renewables more affordable; and helping us get off this damn rock. It hasn't all worked, but making cars less damaging and breaking humanity's dependence on Earth are both part of the same plan and it's disingenuous to try and play them against each other. Reducing the money involved to normal people money for an analogy, it would be like losing your job and both reducing your spend, and spending money on getting another job. Someone complaining you have spent more on getting another job than you saved has completely missed the point. A few years ago, all of Musk's endeavors had saving humanity as a connecting theme. This seems to not be the case more recently with OpenAI, Neuralink and Twitter. Of course it's his money, and his decision what to invest in whether that's saving humanity, a big soapbox, or using the last of our resources as this question tried to imply. One of the things this has taught me it's that while I'm very grateful for the contributions he has made, I don't think humanity should be relying on crazy rich people to save it. A f

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: Why does the man sometimes lose so much after a divorce?
Answer: One reason I've seen is the man underestimated how much work his wife did. He was in an unequal marriage doing perhaps 30% of the housework, and this jumps to 100% after the divorce. People focus on money because that's easy to quantify. Things like managing social connections have often been primarily the wife's responsibility, and that's why many men lose a lot of friends after the divorce.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: Should you contact the authorities if you observe your neighbor serving their prepubescent children wine while enjoying dinner on their outdoor garden patio? Do you agree that alcoholic beverages should not be consumed before puberty?
Answer: There are two very different questions here. Should you tell authorities about your neighbor? Answer: no, unless the kids are in immediate danger Do I approve? Perhaps not. But I'm not going to impose my views on others. Imagine some random person on the other side of the world that you've never met decides to introduce alcohol early. Not your responsibility right? Your neighbor is much the same.

Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: A lazy programmer has to write 337 lines of code in 7 days but does not want to do any more work each day than he has to. What is the fewest number of lines he can write on the day that he performs the most work, i.e. writes the most number of lines?
Answer: Getting your head around something is a huge amount of work. By far the least amount of effort would be to do all the work on the first day (337 lines), and spend the next six days relaxing. A close second is to spend six days doing nothing and write the whole thing on the last day. This will lead to you thinking about the problem for six days, so increases the total effort, but will lead to a much better result. Anything else will involve reading code you wrote the day before and so is far more effort.

Question: What you think about Elon Musk aside, is this a good time to purchase a Tesla Y?
Answer: I'm assuming your question is… you've decided to purchase a Model Y, and are deciding on timing. Do you buy now, or do you wait for some new feature. I grew up during the period personal computers went from 16 kilobytes of RAM through to multiple megabytes. Literally every eighteen months over this time the power of computers would double. You'd talk to people and they'd be holding off their purchase because they were waiting for a maths coprocessor, or an integrated sound chip. Eventually I internalized that you're jumping into a moving platform. You just have to jump when it's the right time for you, regardless of where the industry was at in that day. Buy knowing that a better computer is just around the corner. It's similar with Tesla. I really wanted one after reading about it on the internet, and put my name down as soon as the RHD version was announced. Several years later when the RHD version neared production, the Model 3 was out and was clearly a better fit so I put my name on that instead. Again a year later the Y came out and I shifted to that. As the RHD Y neared release to NZ, I was looking at the Cybertruck, thinking about how rough I am on vehicles and wondering if that would be better. Ultimately the deciding factor for me was a repair bill for my current car. We paid, and my wife said she wanted me to get rid of it so we don't have another bill like that. Every month or so Tesla tweaks the Model Y. Adding features, lowering the price… Waiting always leads to a better deal. Ultimately I think these benefits are incremental — you buy when you've saved up the money, and accept that the month after you've bought there will be a better deal. There's things that annoy me about my car. I'd love better cameras. I'd love more comfortable suspension. I'd love the garage opener to support TCP/IP garages. I'm glad I bought though, because the alternative was keeping my old car with it's minimal storage and constantly worrying that a dashboard light would signal another $5k repair bill.

Question: Which is better for the environment, hydrogen or electric cars?
Answer: Burning hydrogen is fine for the environment. You could quite happily park a hydrogen car in your bedroom, leave the motor on, and not worry about emissions. The trouble with hydrogen is that we can't make it in quantity or distribute it safely without significant environmental damage. It's worse for the environment than oil.

Question: I have seen many people hate the Python indentation style. Why, and what syntax style do you like?
Answer: When I was first taught to program, I was told that style was critically important and showed I understood the problem, while the computer ignored it. It’s part of how the programmer communicates with the next programmer, much like sensible variable names and good comments. There was outrage at the idea of the computer using this whitespace to interpret the language.
